D. By integrating with AWS Chatbot to filter non-critical alerts

**Answer: B.  By correlating multiple weak signals into a single Critical finding with context**

**Explanation:** Extended Threat Detection helps reduce alert fatigue by correlating multiple weak signals and lower-severity events into a single, high-confidence Critical severity finding. Instead of investigating dozens of potentially unrelated events, security teams can focus on consolidated attack sequence findings with full context about the attack stages and involved resources.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty-extended-threat-detection.html

### Iam Fundamentals

#### Iam Fundamentals Q1

What is an IAM user group and what is its primary purpose?

A. A security boundary that limits the maximum permissions an IAM user can have, preventing privilege escalation
B. A collection of IAM users that allows you to specify permissions for multiple users simultaneously
C. A temporary credential provider that generates short-lived tokens for users to assume roles across accounts
D. An authentication mechanism that validates user identity using multi-factor authentication before granting access

**Answer: B.  A collection of IAM users that allows you to specify permissions for multiple users simultaneously**

**Explanation:** An IAM user group is a collection of IAM users that simplifies permission management by allowing you to attach policies to the group. All users in the group automatically receive those permissions, making it easier to manage permissions for multiple users at once.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_groups.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q2

Which statement accurately describes IAM user group limitations?

A. User groups can contain multiple users, and users can belong to multiple groups, but groups cannot be nested
B. User groups can be nested up to three levels deep, and users inherit permissions from all parent groups
C. Each user can belong to only one user group at a time to prevent permission conflicts
D. User groups can contain other groups and IAM roles, allowing for hierarchical permission structures

**Answer: A.  User groups can contain multiple users, and users can belong to multiple groups, but groups cannot be nested**

**Explanation:** IAM user groups can contain many users, and a user can belong to multiple groups. However, user groups cannot be nested - they can only contain users, not other groups. There is no default group that includes all users; you must create and manage group memberships explicitly.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_groups.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q3

Can you specify an IAM user group as a Principal in a resource-based policy?

A. Yes, groups can be specified as principals in resource-based policies for simplified access management
B. Yes, but only for S3 bucket policies and SQS queue policies; other services do not support group principals
C. No, groups relate to permissions not authentication, and principals must be authenticated IAM entities
D. No, unless you enable the 'Allow Groups as Principals' setting in IAM account settings first

**Answer: C.  No, groups relate to permissions not authentication, and principals must be authenticated IAM entities**

**Explanation:** You cannot identify an IAM user group as a Principal in a policy (such as a resource-based policy) because groups relate to permissions, not authentication. Principals are authenticated IAM entities like users, roles, or federated users. To grant resource access to group members, attach identity-based policies to the group.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_groups.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q4

When AWS evaluates identity-based policies and resource-based policies together, how are the resulting permissions determined?

A. The resulting permissions are the intersection; both policy types must explicitly allow an action
B. The resulting permissions are the union; if either policy allows an action, it's allowed (explicit deny overrides)
C. Identity-based policies always take precedence over resource-based policies in case of conflicts
D. Resource-based policies are evaluated first; identity-based policies only apply if resource policies are absent

**Answer: B.  The resulting permissions are the union; if either policy allows an action, it's allowed (explicit deny overrides)**

**Explanation:** When evaluating identity-based and resource-based policies, the resulting permissions are the union of the two. If an action is allowed by an identity-based policy, a resource-based policy, or both, AWS allows the action. However, an explicit deny in either policy overrides any allow.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q5

How does AWS evaluate identity-based policies when a permissions boundary is attached to an IAM user?

A. The resulting permissions are the union; the user gets permissions from both the identity policy and boundary
B. The resulting permissions are the intersection; the boundary limits the maximum permissions the user can have
C. The permissions boundary completely replaces identity-based policies until the boundary is removed
D. Identity-based policies are evaluated first; the permissions boundary only applies if policies grant excessive permissions

**Answer: B.  The resulting permissions are the intersection; the boundary limits the maximum permissions the user can have**

**Explanation:** When AWS evaluates identity-based policies with a permissions boundary, the resulting permissions are the intersection of the two categories. Adding a permissions boundary might reduce the actions a user can perform. An explicit deny in either overrides any allow. This is an advanced feature for enforcing maximum permission limits.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q6

When an IAM user in an AWS Organizations member account accesses a resource without a resource-based policy, which policies determine the resulting permissions?

A. Identity-based policies only; SCPs and RCPs do not apply to IAM users, only to roles
B. Identity-based policies and SCPs only; RCPs apply only to resource-based policies
C. Identity-based policies, SCPs, and RCPs; resulting permissions are the intersection of all three
D. Identity-based policies, SCPs, and RCPs; resulting permissions are the union of all three

**Answer: C.  Identity-based policies, SCPs, and RCPs; resulting permissions are the intersection of all three**

**Explanation:** When a user belongs to an account in an organization and accesses a resource without a resource-based policy, the resulting permissions are the intersection of the user's identity-based policies, Service Control Policies (SCPs), and Resource Control Policies (RCPs). An action must be allowed by all three. An explicit deny in any of these overrides the allow.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q7

What is the difference between an explicit deny and an implicit deny in IAM policy evaluation?

A. Explicit denies can be overridden by higher-priority allow statements; implicit denies are permanent and cannot be overridden
B. Explicit denies result from a Deny statement in an applicable policy; implicit denies occur when no Allow statement exists
C. Explicit denies apply to principal-based policies only; implicit denies apply to resource-based policies only
D. Explicit denies are temporary and expire after 24 hours; implicit denies remain until explicitly allowed

**Answer: B.  Explicit denies result from a Deny statement in an applicable policy; implicit denies occur when no Allow statement exists**

**Explanation:** An explicit deny occurs when an applicable policy includes a Deny statement. An implicit deny occurs when there is no applicable Deny statement and no applicable Allow statement. By default, IAM principals are denied access unless explicitly allowed. Explicit denies always override allows.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q8

What is the fundamental principle of IAM policy evaluation when both Allow and Deny statements apply to a request?

A. The most recently created policy takes precedence, whether it contains Allow or Deny
B. Allow statements take precedence over Deny statements to enable least-privilege access patterns
C. Deny statements always take precedence; if both Allow and Deny apply, the Deny overrides the Allow
D. The policy evaluation engine prompts for administrator approval when conflicting statements exist

**Answer: C.  Deny statements always take precedence; if both Allow and Deny apply, the Deny overrides the Allow**

**Explanation:** The fundamental principle is that an explicit Deny always wins. If an Allow and Deny statement both apply to a request, the Deny statement takes precedence and overrides the Allow. This applies across all policy types including identity-based, resource-based, permissions boundaries, SCPs, and RCPs.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q9

How many MFA devices can be registered for a single IAM user or root user account?

A. Only one MFA device per user to ensure unique authentication credentials
B. Up to two MFA devices: one primary and one backup for redundancy purposes
C. Up to eight MFA devices of any type; only one device is needed to sign in
D. Up to five MFA devices, but virtual MFA apps count separately from hardware devices

**Answer: C.  Up to eight MFA devices of any type; only one device is needed to sign in**

**Explanation:** AWS account root users and IAM users can register up to eight MFA devices of any combination of supported types. Registering multiple devices provides flexibility and reduces access interruption risk if a device is lost or broken. You only need one MFA device to sign in to the console or create a CLI session.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q10

Which MFA types does AWS currently support for IAM users?

A. Passkeys and security keys (FIDO), virtual authenticator applications, and hardware TOTP tokens
B. Virtual authenticator applications, hardware TOTP tokens, and SMS text message-based MFA
C. Passkeys and security keys (FIDO), biometric authentication, and smart card-based MFA
D. Virtual authenticator applications, push notification-based MFA, and USB security keys

**Answer: A.  Passkeys and security keys (FIDO), virtual authenticator applications, and hardware TOTP tokens**

**Explanation:** AWS supports three MFA types: 1) Passkeys and security keys (FIDO2-based device-bound and synced passkeys), 2) Virtual authenticator applications (software-based TOTP), and 3) Hardware TOTP tokens. AWS ended support for enabling SMS text message-based MFA and recommends switching to alternative methods.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q11

What are passkeys and how do they differ from traditional security keys?

A. Passkeys are virtual devices stored in cloud credential managers; security keys are physical hardware devices
B. Passkeys use SMS-based authentication codes; security keys use TOTP algorithms for code generation
C. Passkeys require biometric authentication on every use; security keys only require PIN entry once per session
D. Passkeys are single-use tokens that expire after authentication; security keys are permanent devices

**Answer: A.  Passkeys are virtual devices stored in cloud credential managers; security keys are physical hardware devices**

**Explanation:** Passkeys based on FIDO standards use public key cryptography for phishing-resistant authentication. AWS supports two types: device-bound passkeys (physical security keys like YubiKey) and synced passkeys (stored in credential managers from Google, Apple, Microsoft, 1Password, Dashlane, Bitwarden). Synced passkeys can be backed up and used across devices.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q12

How do virtual authenticator applications implement MFA for AWS?

A. They generate device-unique codes based on the device's hardware serial number that AWS validates server-side
B. They implement the time-based one-time password (TOTP) algorithm and support multiple tokens on a single device
C. They use AWS's proprietary authentication algorithm that syncs with AWS's time servers every 30 seconds
D. They create encrypted connections to AWS IAM service endpoints that validate user biometric data

**Answer: B.  They implement the time-based one-time password (TOTP) algorithm and support multiple tokens on a single device**

**Explanation:** Virtual authenticator applications (like Google Authenticator, Authy) run on phones or other devices and emulate physical MFA devices. They implement the TOTP (time-based one-time password) algorithm defined in RFC 6238 and support multiple tokens on a single device. Each token must be unique to a user.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q13

What limitation applies to hardware TOTP tokens used with AWS accounts?

A. Hardware TOTP tokens expire after 2 years and must be replaced with new devices from AWS-approved vendors
B. Hardware TOTP tokens can only be used with the root user account, not with IAM users for security reasons
C. Hardware TOTP tokens are device-specific to AWS accounts and must be purchased from AWS-approved sources with shared token seeds
D. Hardware TOTP tokens require periodic recalibration every 90 days using a special AWS synchronization utility

**Answer: C.  Hardware TOTP tokens are device-specific to AWS accounts and must be purchased from AWS-approved sources with shared token seeds**

**Explanation:** Hardware TOTP tokens used with AWS are device-specific and can only be used with AWS accounts. They must be purchased from specific AWS-approved sources (specific SafeNet products) because the token seeds (secret keys) must be shared securely with AWS at production time. Tokens from other sources will not work with IAM.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q14

What is a credential report in IAM and what information does it contain?

A. A real-time dashboard showing active sessions, API calls, and resource access patterns for all IAM users
B. A CSV file listing all users in your account and the status of their credentials including passwords, access keys, and MFA devices
C. An encrypted audit log of all authentication attempts, both successful and failed, for compliance reporting
D. A CloudWatch Logs stream containing detailed IAM policy evaluation results for troubleshooting access denials

**Answer: B.  A CSV file listing all users in your account and the status of their credentials including passwords, access keys, and MFA devices**

**Explanation:** A credential report is a CSV file that lists all IAM users in your account and the status of their various credentials including passwords, access keys (first two per user), MFA devices, and X.509 certificates. You can generate reports as frequently as once every four hours for credential auditing.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_getting-report.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q15

Which IAM credentials are included in a credential report?

A. All IAM credentials including passwords, all access keys, MFA devices, X.509 certificates, and service-specific credentials
B. IAM-managed credentials only: passwords, first two access keys per user, MFA devices, and X.509 certificates
C. Active credentials only: currently valid passwords, non-expired access keys, and enabled MFA devices
D. Root user and IAM user credentials including SSH keys, API tokens, and database passwords

**Answer: B.  IAM-managed credentials only: passwords, first two access keys per user, MFA devices, and X.509 certificates**

**Explanation:** Credential reports include IAM-managed credentials: passwords, the first two access keys per user (not additional keys beyond the first two), MFA devices, and X.509 certificates. Service-specific credentials for services like AWS CodeCommit or Amazon Keyspaces are not included in the report.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_getting-report.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q16

What permissions are required to generate and download IAM credential reports?

A. iam:GenerateCredentialReport to create reports; iam:GetCredentialReport to download them
B. iam:CreateReport to generate reports; iam:DownloadReport to retrieve them from S3
C. iam:GenerateReport and iam:ListCredentials to create and access reports
D. Only iam:GetCredentialReport is needed; AWS automatically generates reports every 4 hours

**Answer: A.  iam:GenerateCredentialReport to create reports; iam:GetCredentialReport to download them**

**Explanation:** To generate credential reports, users need iam:GenerateCredentialReport permission. To download and view reports, users need iam:GetCredentialReport permission. These are separate actions to allow separation of duties between report generation and report access.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_getting-report.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q17

How frequently can you generate IAM credential reports?

A. Once every hour; more frequent generation is throttled to prevent API abuse
B. Once every four hours; reports generated more frequently return the most recent existing report
C. Once per day; credential reports are resource-intensive operations with strict rate limits
D. Unlimited frequency; reports are generated on-demand with no throttling or rate limits

**Answer: B.  Once every four hours; reports generated more frequently return the most recent existing report**

**Explanation:** You can generate credential reports as frequently as once every four hours. If you attempt to generate a report more frequently than that, AWS returns the most recently generated report instead of creating a new one. This limit helps manage the computational overhead of report generation.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_getting-report.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q18

What password policy settings can be configured for IAM users?

A. Minimum length, character complexity requirements, password expiration periods, and password reuse prevention
B. Minimum length only; AWS does not support complexity requirements for compatibility with legacy systems
C. All settings including biometric requirements, device binding, and geographic access restrictions
D. Complexity requirements and expiration only; minimum length is fixed at 8 characters per AWS security standards

**Answer: A.  Minimum length, character complexity requirements, password expiration periods, and password reuse prevention**

**Explanation:** AWS allows you to set custom password policies specifying minimum length, complexity requirements (uppercase, lowercase, numbers, non-alphanumeric characters), mandatory password rotation periods, and password reuse prevention. The default policy applies if no custom policy is configured. Password policies do not apply to root users or access keys.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_passwords_account-policy.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q19

When do IAM password policy settings take effect for existing users?

A. Immediately upon policy change; all users must reset passwords within 24 hours to comply with new policy
B. At the next scheduled password rotation; changes do not affect current passwords until expiration
C. On the next password change except for expiration periods which take effect immediately
D. After a 7-day grace period allowing users time to prepare for new password requirements

**Answer: C.  On the next password change except for expiration periods which take effect immediately**

**Explanation:** Password policy settings are enforced at the next password change for existing users, not retroactively on current passwords. The exception is password expiration periods, which take effect immediately after policy changes. This means users with non-compliant passwords can continue using them until they change their password.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_passwords_account-policy.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q20

Which AWS service does AWS recommend for centralized, MFA-protected access management instead of managing individual IAM user credentials?

A. AWS Secrets Manager for storing and rotating IAM user credentials with automatic MFA enforcement
B. AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) for centralized single sign-on with MFA protection
C. AWS Directory Service for Active Directory to manage IAM users through corporate directory federation
D. AWS Control Tower for enforcing MFA policies across all accounts using preventive guardrails

**Answer: B.  AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) for centralized single sign-on with MFA protection**

**Explanation:** AWS recommends IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) for centralized access management. It provides MFA-protected single sign-on access to multiple AWS accounts from one place. You can create identities in IAM Identity Center or connect to existing SAML 2.0 compatible identity providers, reducing the need to manage individual IAM users.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q21

What happens to unassigned virtual MFA devices in your AWS account?

A. They remain indefinitely until manually deleted by an administrator using the IAM console
B. They are automatically deleted when adding new virtual MFA devices, allowing reuse of device names
C. They are archived to S3 Glacier after 90 days of inactivity for compliance and audit purposes
D. They are automatically deactivated but retained for 30 days before permanent deletion

**Answer: B.  They are automatically deleted when adding new virtual MFA devices, allowing reuse of device names**

**Explanation:** Unassigned virtual MFA devices (devices created but not assigned to any root user or IAM user) are automatically deleted when you're adding new virtual MFA devices either via the console or during sign-in. This cleanup allows you to reuse device names and helps manage the number of devices in your account.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q22

Can you use the same FIDO security key for multiple AWS accounts?

A. No, each security key can only be registered to one AWS account for security isolation
B. Yes, a single security key can support multiple root user accounts and IAM users across different AWS accounts
C. Yes, but only for accounts within the same AWS Organization; cross-organization use is not supported
D. No, but you can clone security key credentials to multiple physical devices for multi-account access

**Answer: B.  Yes, a single security key can support multiple root user accounts and IAM users across different AWS accounts**

**Explanation:** A single FIDO security key can support multiple root user accounts and IAM users across different AWS accounts. This makes hardware security keys more practical for users who manage multiple AWS accounts. Each account maintains its own registration, but the same physical key can be used for all of them.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q23

What connectivity methods do FIDO security keys support for authentication with AWS?

A. USB, Bluetooth, and NFC connections; platform authenticators like Touch ID or Face ID can also be used
B. USB connections only; wireless methods are not supported due to security concerns
C. Bluetooth and NFC only; USB connections are deprecated in favor of wireless authentication methods
D. USB and proprietary AWS wireless protocol; standard Bluetooth and NFC are not supported

**Answer: A.  USB, Bluetooth, and NFC connections; platform authenticators like Touch ID or Face ID can also be used**

**Explanation:** FIDO security keys support multiple connectivity methods including USB, Bluetooth, and NFC. Additionally, platform authenticators like Touch ID on MacBooks or Face ID on mobile devices can unlock credential managers to sign in to AWS. This flexibility allows users to choose authentication methods that best fit their devices and workflows.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q24

What is a key limitation when using FIDO security keys with AWS STS API operations?

A. Security keys require interactive browser-based authentication and cannot be used for programmatic STS API calls
B. Security keys can only be used with STS AssumeRole operations, not with GetSessionToken or GetFederationToken
C. Security keys must be re-registered every 30 days when used with STS for temporary credential generation
D. Security keys cannot be used as the primary MFA device; they must be secondary to a virtual MFA device

**Answer: A.  Security keys require interactive browser-based authentication and cannot be used for programmatic STS API calls**

**Explanation:** You cannot pass MFA information for a FIDO security key to AWS STS API operations to request temporary credentials. FIDO security keys require interactive authentication through a browser. For programmatic access requiring MFA, use virtual MFA devices or hardware TOTP tokens instead.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

#### Iam Fundamentals Q25

Why does AWS recommend registering multiple MFA devices for IAM users?

A. Multiple devices improve authentication speed by allowing load balancing across devices during high-traffic periods
B. Multiple devices enable different security levels (low/medium/high) based on the sensitivity of operations being performed
C. Multiple devices provide backup access if one device is lost/stolen and eliminate single points of failure
D. Multiple devices are required for compliance with SOC 2 and ISO 27001 security certification standards

**Answer: C.  Multiple devices provide backup access if one device is lost/stolen and eliminate single points of failure**

**Explanation:** AWS recommends registering multiple MFA devices (up to 8) to raise security while providing backup access. If one device is lost, stolen, or inaccessible, users can authenticate with another device without performing account recovery. This is especially useful for geographically dispersed teams and allows keeping backup hardware devices in secure locations like vaults.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html

### Iam Policies

#### Iam Policies Q1

A user has an identity-based policy that allows s3:*, but an SCP denies s3:DeleteObject. A bucket policy also allows s3:* for the user. Can the user delete objects from the bucket?

A. Yes, because the bucket policy's explicit allow overrides the SCP deny for resource-based access
B. No, because explicit denies in SCPs take precedence over all other policy types
C. Yes, because identity-based and resource-based policies both allow, creating an effective allow
D. No, because resource-based policies cannot override identity-based policy denials

**Answer: B.  No, because explicit denies in SCPs take precedence over all other policy types**

**Explanation:** An explicit deny ALWAYS wins, regardless of which policy type contains it. SCPs are evaluated early in the policy evaluation logic, and a deny in an SCP cannot be overridden by any other policy type - identity-based, resource-based, or otherwise.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html

#### Iam Policies Q2

An S3 bucket in Account B (222222222222) has this bucket policy allowing s3:GetObject for an IAM role in Account A (111111111111): ```json { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/CrossAccountRole"}, "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::account-b-bucket/*" }] } ``` The role in Account A has NO identity-based policies attached. Can the role access objects in the bucket?

A. No, because cross-account access requires BOTH an explicit Allow in the bucket policy AND an explicit Allow in the role's identity-based policy
B. No, because the role has an implicit deny from having no identity-based policies, which cannot be overridden by resource policies
C. Yes, because resource-based policies can grant cross-account access independently without requiring identity-based policies on the role
D. Yes, but only if you also add a trust policy on the role allowing Account B to assume it

**Answer: A.  No, because cross-account access requires BOTH an explicit Allow in the bucket policy AND an explicit Allow in the role's identity-based policy**

**Explanation:** For cross-account access, you need BOTH sides to explicitly Allow: 1. ✅ Resource-based policy (bucket policy) must Allow - this is present 2. ❌ Identity-based policy on the role must Allow - this is MISSING The role needs an identity-based policy like: ```json { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::account-b-bucket/*" }] } ``` Without this, the role has an implicit deny that blocks access. Resource-based policies CAN grant same-account access independently, but cross-account requires explicit Allow on both sides.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html#policy-eval-basics

#### Iam Policies Q3

A DevOps team creates IAM roles for developers. The security team wants to ensure these roles cannot have more permissions than the DevOps team role itself. What should be implemented?

A. An SCP at the organization level that restricts the DevOps team's iam:CreateRole permissions
B. A permissions boundary that the DevOps team must attach to all roles they create
C. A trust policy on the DevOps role that limits which roles it can create
D. An IAM policy on the DevOps role that denies creating roles with AdministratorAccess

**Answer: B.  A permissions boundary that the DevOps team must attach to all roles they create**

**Explanation:** A Permissions Boundary sets the maximum permissions that identity-based policies can grant. By requiring DevOps to attach a boundary to created roles, you ensure those roles cannot exceed the boundary's permissions, preventing privilege escalation.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html

#### Iam Policies Q4

A bucket policy needs to allow access from any IAM principal in Account 123456789012. Which Principal element should be used?

A. 'Principal': { 'AWS': 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root' } to reference the account
B. 'Principal': { 'AWS': '123456789012' } using the account ID directly
C. 'Principal': { 'Account': '123456789012' } using the Account key
D. Both A and B are valid; they are equivalent ways to specify the account as principal

**Answer: D.  Both A and B are valid; they are equivalent ways to specify the account as principal**

**Explanation:** The Principal element specifies who can access a resource. Both 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root' and '123456789012' are valid ways to specify an AWS account as principal. They are functionally equivalent and allow any authenticated principal from that account.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_principal.html

#### Iam Policies Q5

A company wants their S3 bucket to only be accessible by principals from within their AWS Organization (o-xxxxxxxxxx). Which condition should they use?

A. 'aws:PrincipalAccount': 'o-xxxxxxxxxx' to verify the principal's account is in the organization
B. 'aws:PrincipalOrgID': 'o-xxxxxxxxxx' to verify the principal belongs to the organization
C. 'aws:SourceOrgID': 'o-xxxxxxxxxx' to verify the request source organization
D. 'aws:RequestOrgID': 'o-xxxxxxxxxx' to verify the organization making the request

**Answer: B.  'aws:PrincipalOrgID': 'o-xxxxxxxxxx' to verify the principal belongs to the organization**

**Explanation:** aws:PrincipalOrgID checks if the principal making the request belongs to a specific AWS Organization. It's commonly used in resource-based policies to restrict access to only principals within your organization, simplifying cross-account access management.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html#condition-keys-principalorgid

#### Iam Policies Q6

An architect wants to use an IAM group as a principal in an S3 bucket policy to grant access to all group members. Is this possible?

A. Yes, specify the group ARN in the Principal element like other IAM entities
B. Yes, but only if the group has fewer than 100 members due to policy size limits
C. No, groups cannot be specified as principals; you must list individual users or use roles
D. No, but you can specify the group's path instead of ARN as a workaround

**Answer: C.  No, groups cannot be specified as principals; you must list individual users or use roles**

**Explanation:** IAM groups CANNOT be referenced as principals in resource-based policies. Groups can only contain IAM users (not roles), cannot be nested, and don't have credentials. For resource policies, you must specify individual users, roles, or entire accounts.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_groups.html

#### Iam Policies Q7

A security team wants to allow all AWS actions EXCEPT IAM actions. Which policy construct should they use?

A. 'Effect': 'Deny' with 'Action': 'iam:*' to block IAM while allowing everything else
B. 'Effect': 'Allow' with 'NotAction': 'iam:*' to allow everything except IAM actions
C. 'Effect': 'Allow' with 'Action': '*' and a separate 'NotAction': 'iam:*' statement
D. 'Effect': 'Deny' with 'NotAction': 'iam:*' to deny everything except IAM actions

**Answer: B.  'Effect': 'Allow' with 'NotAction': 'iam:*' to allow everything except IAM actions**

**Explanation:** NotAction with Allow matches all actions EXCEPT those specified, effectively allowing everything except IAM. Note that using Deny with NotAction would deny everything except IAM - the opposite of what's wanted.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_notaction.html

#### Iam Policies Q8

A new IAM user is created but no policies are attached. The user tries to list S3 buckets. What happens?

A. The action succeeds because users have read-only access by default
B. The action is denied because of the implicit deny; no permissions are granted by default
C. The action succeeds but only returns buckets with public access enabled
D. The action prompts for MFA verification before granting read access

**Answer: B.  The action is denied because of the implicit deny; no permissions are granted by default**

**Explanation:** By default, IAM users have NO permissions. This is the implicit deny - unless a policy explicitly allows an action, it's denied. The user must have permissions granted through identity-based policies, group membership, or role assumption.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html

#### Iam Policies Q9

A security team needs to identify S3 buckets that are accessible by principals outside their AWS Organization. Which tool should they use?

A. Amazon Macie to scan bucket policies for external access patterns
B. IAM Access Analyzer to identify resources shared outside the zone of trust
C. AWS Config with the s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited rule
D. Amazon GuardDuty to detect unauthorized cross-account access attempts

**Answer: B.  IAM Access Analyzer to identify resources shared outside the zone of trust**

**Explanation:** IAM Access Analyzer identifies resources (S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, etc.) that are shared with external entities outside your zone of trust (account or organization). It continuously monitors and generates findings for resources with external access.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-access-analyzer.html

#### Iam Policies Q10

A company wants to restrict IAM operations to only be allowed from their corporate IP range. Which condition key should be used?

A. 'aws:SourceArn' with the corporate network identifier as the ARN
B. 'aws:SourceIp' with the corporate CIDR range, but note it won't work for service calls
C. 'aws:VpcSourceIp' with the corporate VPC CIDR range for internal network restriction
D. 'aws:CallerIdentity' with IP address validation in the condition

**Answer: B.  'aws:SourceIp' with the corporate CIDR range, but note it won't work for service calls**

**Explanation:** aws:SourceIp restricts API calls based on source IP address or CIDR range. Important caveat: this condition doesn't work for calls made through AWS services on your behalf (like CloudFormation creating resources), as those originate from AWS IPs.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html#condition-keys-sourceip

#### Iam Policies Q11

A policy needs to ensure that EC2 instances can only be launched if they have an 'Environment' tag with value 'Production' or 'Staging'. Which condition key should be used?

A. 'aws:ResourceTag/Environment' to check the Environment tag value on the instance
B. 'aws:RequestTag/Environment' to validate the tag during the RunInstances call
C. 'ec2:TagKeys' to ensure the Environment key is present in the request
D. 'ec2:ResourceTag/Environment' with StringEquals for the allowed values

**Answer: B.  'aws:RequestTag/Environment' to validate the tag during the RunInstances call**

**Explanation:** aws:RequestTag controls tags being APPLIED during resource creation. It validates tags in the RunInstances request. Use aws:ResourceTag to check EXISTING tags on resources. For creation-time enforcement, RequestTag is appropriate.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_tags.html

#### Iam Policies Q12

A delegated admin can create IAM roles for their team. How can you prevent them from creating a role with AdministratorAccess?

A. Use an SCP to deny iam:CreateRole for roles with AdministratorAccess attached
B. Require them to attach a permissions boundary to any role they create, limiting maximum permissions
C. Remove iam:AttachRolePolicy from their permissions so they can only create roles, not attach policies
D. Create a Config rule that deletes roles with AdministratorAccess as soon as they're created

**Answer: B.  Require them to attach a permissions boundary to any role they create, limiting maximum permissions**

**Explanation:** Permissions boundaries prevent privilege escalation by setting maximum permissions for created roles. Even if someone can create roles and attach policies, the boundary limits effective permissions. You can require boundary attachment via IAM policy conditions.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html

#### Iam Policies Q13

A developer can create EC2 instances but receives 'not authorized to perform iam:PassRole' when trying to launch an instance with an IAM role. What's missing?

A. The developer needs sts:AssumeRole permission to use the role with EC2
B. The developer needs iam:PassRole permission to pass the role to the EC2 service
C. The EC2 service needs to be added to the role's trust policy as a principal
D. The developer needs iam:CreateServiceLinkedRole to link the role to EC2

**Answer: B.  The developer needs iam:PassRole permission to pass the role to the EC2 service**

**Explanation:** iam:PassRole controls who can pass an IAM role to an AWS service. The developer needs explicit iam:PassRole permission (typically scoped to specific role ARNs) to configure EC2 instances with IAM roles. This is a common delegation control.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_passrole.html

#### Iam Policies Q14

A Lambda function in Account A needs to access a DynamoDB table in Account B. Which approach is MOST straightforward?

A. Create an SCP in the Organization that allows cross-account DynamoDB access between the accounts
B. Add a resource-based policy to the DynamoDB table allowing the Lambda role from Account A
C. Create a role in Account B that Account A's Lambda can assume, with permissions to the DynamoDB table
D. Configure VPC peering between accounts and use VPC endpoint policies for cross-account access

**Answer: C.  Create a role in Account B that Account A's Lambda can assume, with permissions to the DynamoDB table**

**Explanation:** DynamoDB doesn't support resource-based policies. For cross-account access, the standard approach is creating a role in Account B with DynamoDB permissions, then configuring the Lambda to assume that role. This works for services without resource policies.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies-cross-account-resource-access.html

#### Iam Policies Q15

A security architect is designing policies for a complex application. What is the maximum size for an IAM managed policy?

A. 2,048 characters, matching the inline policy limit for efficiency
B. 5,120 characters, the same limit as Service Control Policies
C. 6,144 characters (approximately 6 KB) including all whitespace
D. 10,240 characters, doubled from inline policies for managed use cases

**Answer: C.  6,144 characters (approximately 6 KB) including all whitespace**

**Explanation:** IAM managed policies have a maximum size of 6,144 characters (approximately 6 KB). This includes all whitespace. Inline policies have a smaller limit (2,048). SCPs have 5,120. If you exceed limits, split into multiple policies or optimize the policy structure.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_iam-quotas.html

#### Iam Policies Q16

A policy denies actions unless 'aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent' is true. An IAM user authenticates with MFA and gets console access, then generates access keys from the console. Can they make API calls with those keys?

A. Yes, because MFA was used to access the console where the keys were created
B. No, because long-term access keys don't have aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent in requests
C. Yes, but only within the same session that was used to create the keys
D. No, because access keys cannot be created when MFA policies are in effect

**Answer: B.  No, because long-term access keys don't have aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent in requests**

**Explanation:** aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent checks the CURRENT request's authentication. Long-term access keys don't carry MFA context - the condition key is NOT PRESENT (not false, but missing). The user would need to use GetSessionToken with MFA to get temporary credentials that satisfy this condition.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa_configure-api-require.html

#### Iam Policies Q17

A bucket policy specifies 'Principal': { 'AWS': 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:group/Developers' }. What is the effect?

A. All members of the Developers group can access the bucket as intended
B. The policy is invalid because groups cannot be principals; it will cause access denied errors
C. Only the group creator can access the bucket, not the group members
D. The policy grants access to a role named 'group/Developers' if one exists

**Answer: B.  The policy is invalid because groups cannot be principals; it will cause access denied errors**

**Explanation:** IAM groups CANNOT be specified as principals in policies. Group ARNs in Principal elements are invalid. You must specify individual users, roles, or account roots. Policies with invalid principals may cause unexpected access denied errors.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_principal.html

#### Iam Policies Q18

A security team wants to create a least-privilege policy for a production Lambda function that has been running for 90 days. Which tool can help?

A. IAM Policy Simulator to test what permissions the Lambda currently uses
B. IAM Access Analyzer policy generation to analyze CloudTrail and create a policy based on actual usage
C. AWS Trusted Advisor to recommend permission reductions based on best practices
D. CloudWatch Logs Insights to query Lambda execution logs for API calls made

**Answer: B.  IAM Access Analyzer policy generation to analyze CloudTrail and create a policy based on actual usage**

**Explanation:** IAM Access Analyzer policy generation analyzes CloudTrail logs to identify actions, resources, and conditions actually used. It then generates a least-privilege policy based on that observed activity, perfect for reducing overly permissive policies.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access-analyzer-policy-generation.html

#### Iam Policies Q19

A complex IAM policy has multiple statements. How can you make the policy easier to understand when troubleshooting?

A. Add 'Version' elements to each statement to track policy versions
B. Add 'Sid' (Statement ID) elements with descriptive identifiers for each statement
C. Add 'Comment' elements to each statement explaining its purpose
D. Add 'Description' fields to document what each statement accomplishes

**Answer: B.  Add 'Sid' (Statement ID) elements with descriptive identifiers for each statement**

**Explanation:** Sid (Statement ID) is an optional identifier you can add to each policy statement. Use descriptive names like 'AllowS3ReadAccess' or 'DenyUnencryptedUploads'. This helps identify which statement affects access during troubleshooting. Note: Comment and Description aren't valid policy elements.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_sid.html

#### Iam Policies Q20

A company wants to require MFA for API calls to delete S3 objects, but the MFA must have been used within the last 5 minutes. Which condition should they use?

A. 'aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent': 'true' with 'aws:TokenIssueTime' for recency check
B. 'aws:MultiFactorAuthAge' with NumericLessThan 300 seconds to require recent MFA
C. 'aws:MultiFactorAuthTimestamp' with DateEquals for current-day validation
D. 'aws:SessionDuration' with NumericLessThan 300 to limit session length

**Answer: B.  'aws:MultiFactorAuthAge' with NumericLessThan 300 seconds to require recent MFA**

**Explanation:** aws:MultiFactorAuthAge checks how many seconds have passed since MFA authentication. Using NumericLessThan with 300 requires the MFA to have been used within the last 5 minutes. This is useful for requiring fresh MFA for sensitive operations.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa_configure-api-require.html

#### Iam Policies Q21

AWS creates a role named 'AWSServiceRoleForECS' in your account when you use ECS. You want to modify its permissions. Can you?

A. Yes, modify the attached policies like any other role you own
B. No, service-linked roles have AWS-managed permissions that cannot be modified
C. Yes, but only by contacting AWS Support to request permission changes
D. No, but you can create a custom role with the same trust policy and different permissions

**Answer: B.  No, service-linked roles have AWS-managed permissions that cannot be modified**

**Explanation:** Service-linked roles are predefined IAM roles that AWS services create. They include all permissions the service requires and CANNOT be modified. You can view their policies and delete them when no longer needed, but you cannot change their permissions.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/using-service-linked-roles.html

#### Iam Policies Q22

A security policy requires that all S3 API calls must be made over HTTPS. Which bucket policy condition enforces this?

A. 'aws:SecureTransport': 'true' in an Allow statement to permit only HTTPS requests
B. 'aws:SecureTransport': 'false' in a Deny statement to block HTTP requests
C. 's3:x-amz-server-side-encryption': 'aws:kms' to require encrypted connections
D. 'aws:EncryptionContext': 'true' in a Condition to require transport encryption

**Answer: B.  'aws:SecureTransport': 'false' in a Deny statement to block HTTP requests**

**Explanation:** Use 'aws:SecureTransport': 'false' in a DENY statement to block HTTP requests. This denies when SecureTransport is false (HTTP), effectively requiring HTTPS. Using 'true' in Allow doesn't prevent HTTP since explicit denies are needed to block actions.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html#condition-keys-securetransport

#### Iam Policies Q23

A role's trust policy allows 'Principal': {'Service': 'lambda.amazonaws.com'}. A Lambda function tries to assume a different role using this role's credentials. Can it?

A. Yes, because Lambda is trusted by the role's trust policy
B. No, the trust policy only allows Lambda service to assume the role, not principals using the role
C. Yes, but only if the target role also trusts lambda.amazonaws.com
D. No, because Lambda functions cannot call sts:AssumeRole

**Answer: B.  No, the trust policy only allows Lambda service to assume the role, not principals using the role**

**Explanation:** A trust policy defines who can ASSUME the role, not what the role can do after assumption. The Lambda service can assume this role to run functions. For the Lambda to assume another role, that OTHER role's trust policy must allow the Lambda's role as principal.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_terms-and-concepts.html

#### Iam Policies Q24

An SNS topic receives messages from S3 bucket notifications. How do you ensure the SNS topic only accepts messages from YOUR S3 bucket, not an attacker's?

A. Use 'aws:PrincipalOrgID' to verify S3 is in your organization
B. Use 'aws:SourceArn' or 'aws:SourceAccount' to verify which bucket triggered the notification
C. Use 'aws:CalledVia' to verify the call chain includes s3.amazonaws.com
D. Use 'aws:PrincipalServiceName' to verify the calling service is S3

**Answer: B.  Use 'aws:SourceArn' or 'aws:SourceAccount' to verify which bucket triggered the notification**

**Explanation:** aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount prevent the confused deputy problem by verifying WHICH specific resource triggered the service-to-service call. This ensures SNS only accepts notifications from your bucket ARN, not an attacker's bucket configured to notify your topic.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/confused-deputy.html

#### Iam Policies Q25

An IAM role has 10 managed policies attached. The team needs to add another set of permissions. What are their options?

A. Request a service limit increase to attach more than 10 managed policies
B. Consolidate existing policies to make room, or add an inline policy which has a separate limit
C. Create a second role with the additional permissions and switch between roles as needed
D. All of the above are valid options for adding more permissions to the role

**Answer: D.  All of the above are valid options for adding more permissions to the role**

**Explanation:** The default limit is 10 managed policies per role. Options include: requesting a quota increase, consolidating existing policies, using inline policies (separate limit), or creating additional roles. All approaches are valid depending on your use case.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_iam-quotas.html

### Identity Center Federation

#### Identity Center Federation Q1

A company is migrating from AWS SSO to the renamed service. What documentation references should they update?

A. Change all references from 'AWS IAM' to 'IAM Identity Center' in their runbooks
B. Change all references from 'AWS SSO' to 'IAM Identity Center' in their documentation
C. Change all references from 'AWS Directory Service' to 'IAM Identity Center'
D. No changes needed - AWS SSO and IAM Identity Center are different services

**Answer: B.  Change all references from 'AWS SSO' to 'IAM Identity Center' in their documentation**

**Explanation:** IAM Identity Center was previously known as AWS Single Sign-On (AWS SSO). It was renamed in 2022 to better reflect its role as the central place to manage workforce identity and access to AWS accounts and applications. The service functionality remains the same.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/what-is.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q2

A company uses Okta as their corporate identity provider and wants to integrate with IAM Identity Center. Which identity sources are supported?

A. Only AWS Managed Microsoft AD or self-managed Active Directory through AD Connector
B. Identity Center's built-in directory, Active Directory (Managed AD or AD Connector), or external SAML 2.0 IdP like Okta
C. Only the built-in Identity Center directory with manual user provisioning
D. External OAuth 2.0 providers and on-premises LDAP directories via direct integration

**Answer: B.  Identity Center's built-in directory, Active Directory (Managed AD or AD Connector), or external SAML 2.0 IdP like Okta**

**Explanation:** IAM Identity Center supports three identity sources: its built-in Identity Center directory, AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector (Active Directory), and external identity providers via SAML 2.0 (like Okta, Azure AD, Ping Identity).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/manage-your-identity-source.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q3

An administrator assigns the 'PowerUserAccess' permission set to a user for a specific AWS account. What happens in that account?

A. An IAM user is created in the account with the PowerUserAccess managed policy attached
B. An IAM role is created in the account with policies defined by the permission set, which the user assumes
C. An IAM group is created and the user's Identity Center identity is added as a member
D. A resource-based policy is attached to all resources granting the user PowerUserAccess

**Answer: B.  An IAM role is created in the account with policies defined by the permission set, which the user assumes**

**Explanation:** A Permission Set is a template that defines what policies will be applied. When assigned to a user/group for an account, Identity Center creates an IAM role in that account with those policies. Users assume this role when accessing the account.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/permissionsetsconcept.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q4

A security architect is designing SAML 2.0 federation with AWS. Which flow correctly describes the authentication process?

A. User requests AWS credentials first, then AWS redirects to IdP for validation, then IdP returns approval to AWS
B. User authenticates with the corporate IdP first, IdP generates a SAML assertion, AWS STS validates it and returns temporary credentials
C. User provides corporate credentials directly to AWS, which forwards them to the IdP for validation via LDAP
D. AWS generates a SAML request, IdP signs it with the user's credentials, and AWS validates the signature

**Answer: B.  User authenticates with the corporate IdP first, IdP generates a SAML assertion, AWS STS validates it and returns temporary credentials**

**Explanation:** In SAML 2.0 federation, users authenticate with their corporate identity provider (IdP) first. The IdP then generates a SAML assertion containing user attributes. AWS STS validates the assertion against the trusted provider and returns temporary credentials.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_providers_saml.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q5

A user needs to access multiple AWS accounts and third-party applications using their corporate credentials. Which component provides this capability?

A. The AWS Management Console with cross-account role switching configured for each account
B. The AWS access portal where users sign in once to see all assigned accounts and applications
C. The IAM dashboard with federated access links for each target account
D. The AWS Organizations console with direct links to member account consoles

**Answer: B.  The AWS access portal where users sign in once to see all assigned accounts and applications**

**Explanation:** The AWS access portal is a web-based portal where users sign in once and see all their assigned AWS accounts and applications. From here, they can launch the console or get CLI credentials for any account they have access to.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/using-the-portal.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q6

A company wants to automatically sync user accounts from Azure AD to IAM Identity Center. Which protocols does Identity Center use for this?

A. OAuth 2.0 for authentication and LDAP for user provisioning and synchronization
B. SAML 2.0 for authentication and SCIM for automatic user and group provisioning
C. OpenID Connect for both authentication and user lifecycle management
D. Kerberos for authentication and Microsoft Graph API for directory synchronization

**Answer: B.  SAML 2.0 for authentication and SCIM for automatic user and group provisioning**

**Explanation:** IAM Identity Center uses SAML 2.0 for authentication with external identity providers. It also supports SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) for automatic provisioning and deprovisioning of users and groups from your IdP.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/provision-automatically.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q7

A developer is implementing programmatic access using SAML federation. Which AWS STS API should they call after receiving the SAML assertion?

A. sts:AssumeRole with the SAML assertion included in the RoleSessionName parameter
B. sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML with the SAML assertion, role ARN, and principal ARN
C. sts:GetFederationToken with the SAML assertion as the identity proof
D. sts:GetSessionToken with the SAML assertion to elevate the current session

**Answer: B.  sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML with the SAML assertion, role ARN, and principal ARN**

**Explanation:** AssumeRoleWithSAML is the STS API used for SAML 2.0 federation. It takes the base64-encoded SAML assertion, role ARN, and SAML provider principal ARN. The role must have a trust policy that allows the SAML provider.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRoleWithSAML.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q8

A security team wants users to re-authenticate after 4 hours when using Identity Center. What should they configure?

A. Set the IAM role maximum session duration to 4 hours in each target account
B. Configure the permission set session duration to 4 hours (sessions are configurable from 1-12 hours)
C. Set the Identity Center global session timeout to 4 hours in organizational settings
D. Configure the IdP SAML assertion lifetime to 4 hours in the identity provider settings

**Answer: B.  Configure the permission set session duration to 4 hours (sessions are configurable from 1-12 hours)**

**Explanation:** IAM Identity Center session duration is configurable from 1 to 12 hours per permission set. The default is 1 hour. This controls how long users can access accounts before needing to re-authenticate through the access portal.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/howtosessionduration.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q9

A company wants to grant access to resources based on user attributes like department and cost center from their IdP. Which approach should they use?

A. Create separate permission sets for each department and manually assign users to the appropriate sets
B. Use attribute-based access control (ABAC) with IdP attributes passed through and used in policy conditions
C. Configure resource-based policies on each AWS resource with principal conditions for department values
D. Create IAM groups in each account matching department names and sync group membership from the IdP

**Answer: B.  Use attribute-based access control (ABAC) with IdP attributes passed through and used in policy conditions**

**Explanation:** ABAC uses identity attributes (like department, job code, or cost center) passed from your IdP to make access control decisions. You can create permission sets that use these attributes in policy conditions, enabling dynamic, fine-grained access control.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/abac.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q10

A user authenticated through QuickSight needs to access S3 data with their corporate identity preserved for audit purposes. Which feature enables this?

A. Cross-account role assumption with session tags containing the user's QuickSight identity
B. Trusted Identity Propagation, which passes user identity context between AWS services
C. Resource-based policies on S3 buckets that trust the QuickSight service principal
D. IAM Identity Center permission sets that include both QuickSight and S3 access

**Answer: B.  Trusted Identity Propagation, which passes user identity context between AWS services**

**Explanation:** Trusted Identity Propagation allows user identity to be passed between AWS services without re-authentication. A user in QuickSight can access S3 or Redshift with their identity preserved, enabling fine-grained access control and audit logging.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/trustedidentitypropagation.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q11

A security administrator needs to enable IAM Identity Center for their AWS Organization. Where can this be done?

A. From any member account with IAM administrator permissions for that account
B. Only from the management account or a designated delegated administrator account
C. From the AWS Organizations console in any account with OrganizationsFullAccess policy
D. Only from the management account; delegated administration is not supported for Identity Center

**Answer: B.  Only from the management account or a designated delegated administrator account**

**Explanation:** IAM Identity Center must be enabled in the AWS Organizations management account or a delegated administrator account. Once enabled, it can manage access to all accounts in the organization from a central location.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/getting-started.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q12

A mobile application needs to allow users to sign in with their Google accounts to access AWS resources. Which federation type should be used?

A. SAML 2.0 federation with Google configured as the SAML identity provider
B. Web identity federation using Google's OIDC-compatible authentication
C. IAM Identity Center with Google Workspace configured as the identity source
D. Custom identity broker that exchanges Google tokens for IAM access keys

**Answer: B.  Web identity federation using Google's OIDC-compatible authentication**

**Explanation:** Web identity federation allows users to authenticate using social identity providers (Google, Facebook, Amazon) or any OIDC-compatible IdP. It's commonly used in mobile and web applications to grant users access to AWS resources.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_providers_oidc.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q13

A developer is implementing web identity federation for a mobile app. After receiving an OIDC token from Google, which STS API should they call?

A. sts:AssumeRole with the OIDC token provided as the external ID parameter
B. sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML after converting the OIDC token to SAML format
C. sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with the OIDC token and the role ARN
D. sts:GetFederationToken with the OIDC token as the user identity proof

**Answer: C.  sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with the OIDC token and the role ARN**

**Explanation:** AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is used for web identity federation. It takes an OIDC token from an identity provider (like Google or Cognito) and returns temporary AWS credentials. The role must have a trust policy that allows the OIDC provider.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/STS/latest/APIReference/API_AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q14

An IAM user needs to perform sensitive operations that require MFA but wants to continue using their current identity. Which STS API should they use?

A. AssumeRole with their own role ARN and MFA token to get elevated credentials
B. GetSessionToken with MFA parameters to get temporary credentials for their current identity
C. AssumeRoleWithSAML with MFA assertion to prove their identity with multi-factor
D. GetFederationToken with MFA token to create temporary credentials for API access

**Answer: B.  GetSessionToken with MFA parameters to get temporary credentials for their current identity**

**Explanation:** GetSessionToken returns temporary credentials for your current IAM user identity, commonly used for MFA-protected API access. AssumeRole is for switching to a different role. GetSessionToken preserves your identity while adding MFA protection.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_temp.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q15

A company enabled SCIM between Okta and IAM Identity Center. When a user is terminated in Okta, what happens in Identity Center?

A. The user must be manually removed from Identity Center to revoke access to AWS accounts
B. SCIM automatically deprovisions the user from Identity Center, removing their AWS access
C. The user's permissions are suspended but the account remains until manually deleted
D. Nothing happens - SCIM only handles initial user creation, not lifecycle management

**Answer: B.  SCIM automatically deprovisions the user from Identity Center, removing their AWS access**

**Explanation:** SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management) enables automatic provisioning AND deprovisioning of users and groups. When users are removed from your IdP, SCIM automatically removes them from Identity Center, revoking their AWS access.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/provision-automatically.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q16

A developer wants to use AWS CLI to access multiple accounts through Identity Center without managing access keys. What should they do?

A. Download static access keys from the access portal and configure them in each CLI profile
B. Use 'aws configure sso' with AWS CLI v2 to set up SSO-enabled profiles with automatic credential refresh
C. Create an IAM user in each account and use 'aws configure' with those user's access keys
D. Export credentials from the console session and paste them into environment variables

**Answer: B.  Use 'aws configure sso' with AWS CLI v2 to set up SSO-enabled profiles with automatic credential refresh**

**Explanation:** AWS CLI v2 integrates with IAM Identity Center. Users run 'aws configure sso' to set up profiles that authenticate through the access portal and automatically obtain temporary credentials without managing long-term access keys.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-configure-sso.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q17

An architect is setting up SAML federation directly with IAM (not Identity Center). What IAM resource must they create to establish trust with their IdP?

A. An IAM SAML identity provider resource containing the IdP's SAML metadata document
B. An IAM role with the IdP's public key embedded in the trust policy
C. An IAM user designated as the federation broker for the external IdP
D. An IAM OIDC provider configured with the IdP's SAML endpoint URLs

**Answer: A.  An IAM SAML identity provider resource containing the IdP's SAML metadata document**

**Explanation:** An IAM SAML provider is a resource that describes an external IdP. It contains the IdP's SAML metadata (including its signing certificate). You reference this provider ARN in role trust policies to enable SAML federation.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_providers_create_saml.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q18

A user's Identity Center session expires after 4 hours. They have an AWS console tab still open. What happens?

A. All open console sessions are immediately terminated and the user is logged out
B. The user must re-authenticate through the access portal to get new credentials for new operations
C. Their console session continues indefinitely since it has its own session management
D. Access is temporarily suspended until the session auto-renews in the background

**Answer: B.  The user must re-authenticate through the access portal to get new credentials for new operations**

**Explanation:** When an Identity Center session expires, users must re-authenticate through the access portal to obtain new temporary credentials. Active console sessions may persist briefly due to their own session tokens, but new sessions require re-authentication.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/howtosessionduration.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q19

A company has AWS accounts outside their Organization that they want to include in their SSO solution. How can Identity Center help?

A. It cannot - Identity Center only works with accounts within the same AWS Organization
B. Configure the external accounts as custom SAML 2.0 applications in Identity Center
C. Invite the external accounts to join the Organization before enabling Identity Center access
D. Create IAM users in the external accounts and sync them with Identity Center's directory

**Answer: B.  Configure the external accounts as custom SAML 2.0 applications in Identity Center**

**Explanation:** While Identity Center primarily manages access to organization accounts, you can configure external AWS accounts as custom SAML 2.0 applications. This allows Identity Center to provide SSO to accounts outside your organization.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/saml-custom-idp.html

#### Identity Center Federation Q20

A security team is evaluating whether to use IAM Identity Center or create IAM users in each account. What are the key advantages of Identity Center?

A. IAM users provide better security isolation since each account has independent identity management
B. Identity Center provides centralized management, SSO across accounts, and eliminates long-term credentials in member accounts
C. IAM Identity Center costs less per user compared to IAM users which have licensing fees
D. IAM users support MFA while Identity Center only supports single-factor authentication

**Answer: B.  Identity Center provides centralized management, SSO across accounts, and eliminates long-term credentials in member accounts**

**Explanation:** IAM Identity Center provides centralized identity management, single sign-on across all accounts, automatic credential rotation, and eliminates long-term credentials in each account. IAM users would require separate management in each account.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/what-is.html

### Imagebuilder Ssm

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q1

What is the primary purpose of EC2 Image Builder?

A. To scale EC2 capacity and balance workloads across availability zones
B. To automate the creation, management, and deployment of customized, secure server images
C. To monitor EC2 performance metrics and generate operational CloudWatch alerts
D. To configure EC2 networking rules and manage VPC security group assignments

**Answer: B.  To automate the creation, management, and deployment of customized, secure server images**

**Explanation:** EC2 Image Builder is a fully managed AWS service that automates the creation, management, and deployment of customized, secure, and up-to-date server images (AMIs and container images). It helps you maintain consistent, compliant images across your infrastructure.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/imagebuilder/latest/userguide/what-is-image-builder.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q2

Which components make up an EC2 Image Builder pipeline?

A. Image recipe, distribution settings, and compliance scan results
B. Image recipe, infrastructure configuration, and distribution configuration
C. Base AMI, build components, and assigned security group settings
D. Build instance type, IAM roles, and image lifecycle policies

**Answer: B.  Image recipe, infrastructure configuration, and distribution configuration**

**Explanation:** An Image Builder pipeline consists of three main components: an image recipe (defines base image and components), infrastructure configuration (defines where/how to build), and distribution configuration (defines how to distribute the resulting image across Regions and accounts).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/imagebuilder/latest/userguide/how-image-builder-works.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q3

What types of images can EC2 Image Builder create?

A. Only Amazon Machine Images (AMIs)
B. Only Docker container images
C. Both AMIs and Docker container images
D. Only EC2 instance snapshots

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/imagebuilder/latest/userguide/what-is-image-builder.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q4

How can you share EC2 Image Builder resources with other AWS accounts?

A. Export resources to S3 and import them manually into each target account
B. Using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share with accounts or Organizations
C. Publish the resources publicly through the AWS Marketplace service catalog
D. Deploy cross-account IAM roles with explicit Image Builder resource permissions

**Answer: B.  Using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share with accounts or Organizations**

**Explanation:** EC2 Image Builder integrates with AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) to share specific resources (components, images, image recipes, and container recipes) with any AWS account or through AWS Organizations, enabling centralized image management.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/imagebuilder/latest/userguide/what-is-image-builder.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q5

What security feature does EC2 Image Builder provide for regulated industries?

A. Automated vulnerability scanning integrated with Amazon Inspector findings
B. Pre-configured STIG hardening components for regulated compliance standards
C. Real-time threat detection powered by GuardDuty behavioral analysis rules
D. Network-level DDoS protection applied to the image build infrastructure

**Answer: B.  Pre-configured STIG hardening components for regulated compliance standards**

**Explanation:** Image Builder provides collections of Amazon-managed STIG (Security Technical Implementation Guide) hardening components for companies in regulated industries. These settings help you quickly build compliant images that meet STIG standards without manual configuration.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/imagebuilder/latest/userguide/what-is-image-builder.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q6

What is AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager primarily designed to do?

A. Monitor system performance metrics and generate operational CloudWatch dashboards
B. Automate the process of patching managed nodes with security and other updates
C. Manage IAM permission boundaries and enforce least-privilege access control policies
D. Configure network routing tables and manage VPC security group rule assignments

**Answer: B.  Automate the process of patching managed nodes with security and other updates**

**Explanation:** Patch Manager automates the process of patching managed nodes (EC2 instances, edge devices, on-premises servers, and VMs) with both security-related updates and other types of updates. It provides centralized control, compliance reporting, and cross-platform support.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q7

What is a patch baseline in Patch Manager?

A. A point-in-time snapshot of system state captured before each patch run
B. A configuration that defines rules for which patches are approved for installation
C. A versioned catalog of all patches available from OS vendors and AWS
D. A recurring cron expression that determines when patching tasks are executed

**Answer: B.  A configuration that defines rules for which patches are approved for installation**

**Explanation:** A patch baseline is a configuration that specifies rules for auto-approving patches within days of their release, along with approved and rejected patch lists. It defines what constitutes patch compliance for managed nodes in your organization, not AWS or OS vendors.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q8

What is the recommended method for configuring patching operations in Patch Manager?

A. Manual patching through SSH
B. Patch policies in Quick Setup
C. Custom Lambda functions
D. Direct API calls

**Answer: B.  Patch policies in Quick Setup**

**Explanation:** Patch policies in Quick Setup is the recommended method. Using a single patch policy configuration, you can define patching for all accounts in all Regions in your organization, for only the accounts and Regions you choose, or for a single account-Region pair.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q9

Can Patch Manager upgrade major versions of operating systems?

A. Yes, for all operating systems
B. Yes, but only for Linux distributions
C. No, major OS version upgrades are not supported
D. Yes, but only for Windows Server

**Answer: C.  No, major OS version upgrades are not supported**

**Explanation:** Patch Manager does NOT support upgrading major versions of operating systems, such as Windows Server 2016 to 2019, or RHEL 7 to RHEL 8. It's designed for patch management and minor version upgrades on Linux, not major OS version migrations.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q10

What types of managed nodes can Patch Manager patch?

A. Only EC2 instances running inside your AWS account and VPC
B. Only on-premises servers registered as managed instances via activation codes
C. EC2 instances, edge devices, on-premises servers, and virtual machines
D. Only Linux-based systems running in AWS or hybrid on-premises environments

**Answer: C.  EC2 instances, edge devices, on-premises servers, and virtual machines**

**Explanation:** Patch Manager can patch fleets of Amazon EC2 instances, edge devices, on-premises servers, and virtual machines (VMs) by operating system type. This includes multiple supported operating systems: Windows Server, various Linux distributions, and macOS.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager.html
