#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q11

What is the primary security benefit of AWS Systems Manager Session Manager?

A. Provides faster encrypted SSH connections without periodic certificate rotation overhead
B. Enables secure node management without open inbound ports, bastion hosts, or SSH keys
C. Automatically patches security vulnerabilities identified during active session scans
D. Scans running processes for malware using built-in antivirus engine signature updates

**Answer: B.  Enables secure node management without open inbound ports, bastion hosts, or SSH keys**

**Explanation:** Session Manager's main security benefit is enabling secure node management without opening inbound SSH/RDP ports, maintaining bastion hosts, or managing SSH keys. This reduces attack surface by closing inbound ports while providing centralized IAM-based access control.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q12

How does Session Manager control access to managed nodes?

A. Using SSH keys stored in S3
B. Through IAM policies only
C. Using bastion host credentials
D. Through network ACLs

**Answer: B.  Through IAM policies only**

**Explanation:** Session Manager provides centralized access control through IAM policies only. Administrators grant or revoke access to managed nodes using IAM policies, controlling which users/groups can use Session Manager and which nodes they can access, eliminating SSH key management.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q13

What types of nodes can you connect to using Session Manager?

A. Only EC2 instances running in your AWS account within a single region
B. Only on-premises servers configured with a direct AWS network connection
C. Both EC2 instances and non-EC2 nodes in hybrid/multicloud environments
D. Only Windows Server instances with RDP port access explicitly enabled

**Answer: C.  Both EC2 instances and non-EC2 nodes in hybrid/multicloud environments**

**Explanation:** Session Manager can connect to both Amazon EC2 instances and non-EC2 managed nodes in hybrid and multicloud environments. For non-EC2 nodes, you must activate the advanced-instances tier (which has a charge), but there's no additional charge for EC2 instances.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q14

What Session Manager feature allows you to access applications running inside a managed node?

A. SSH tunneling
B. Port forwarding
C. VPN connection
D. Direct application access

**Answer: B.  Port forwarding**

**Explanation:** Port forwarding allows you to redirect any port inside your managed node to a local port on your client. After that, you can connect to the local port and access server applications running inside the node without opening inbound ports on the instance.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q15

Which services can Session Manager integrate with for logging session activity?

A. CloudTrail only, capturing all API-level session management calls made
B. CloudWatch Logs and S3 only, for storing encrypted session transcript data
C. CloudTrail, S3, CloudWatch Logs, and EventBridge with SNS
D. CloudWatch Logs only, for real-time command monitoring and metric filtering

**Answer: C.  CloudTrail, S3, CloudWatch Logs, and EventBridge with SNS**

**Explanation:** Session Manager integrates with multiple AWS services for logging: CloudTrail (API calls), Amazon S3 (session log data), CloudWatch Logs (monitoring and debugging), and EventBridge with SNS (notifications for session start/stop events). This provides comprehensive audit capabilities.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q16

What is a key limitation of Session Manager logging?

A. Session logs cannot be stored in S3 buckets located in different AWS regions
B. Logging is not available for port forwarding or SSH connections through Session Manager
C. Only the session start and end timestamps are captured, not individual commands run
D. Windows-based session logging is unsupported across several available AWS regions

**Answer: B.  Logging is not available for port forwarding or SSH connections through Session Manager**

**Explanation:** Logging is NOT available for Session Manager sessions that connect through port forwarding or SSH. This is because SSH encrypts all session data within the secure TLS connection, and Session Manager only serves as a tunnel for SSH connections, making logging impossible.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q17

In EC2 Image Builder, what are build components used for?

A. To specify EC2 instance types and sizes used during the image build process
B. To customize settings and scripts applied to the base image during creation
C. To define target AWS Regions and accounts where the final image is distributed
D. To execute post-build automated tests against images before they are released

**Answer: B.  To customize settings and scripts applied to the base image during creation**

**Explanation:** Build components are scripts and customizations that Image Builder applies to your base image. They can add/remove software, customize settings, apply security configurations, and run scripts. Components are reusable building blocks that you can version and share.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/imagebuilder/latest/userguide/how-image-builder-works.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q18

What validation capability does EC2 Image Builder provide before distributing images?

A. Security scans using Amazon Inspector run only during the active build phase
B. Test components that validate images against configured checks before distribution
C. Manual approval gates requiring a designated reviewer before each distribution run
D. Automatic rollback to the previous image version if any build pipeline stage fails

**Answer: B.  Test components that validate images against configured checks before distribution**

**Explanation:** Image Builder provides test components that you can use to validate images before deployment. You can use AWS-provided test components or create custom test components with AWSTOE. Image Builder only distributes your image if all configured tests succeed, ensuring quality and compliance.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/imagebuilder/latest/userguide/what-is-image-builder.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q19

What is a maintenance window in the context of Patch Manager?

A. The time window during which patch content is downloaded to managed nodes
B. A scheduled period for performing patching operations on managed nodes
C. The elapsed time between consecutive patch release cycles from OS vendors
D. The automatic reboot window triggered immediately after patch installation completes

**Answer: B.  A scheduled period for performing patching operations on managed nodes**

**Explanation:** A maintenance window is a scheduled time period where patching operations (and other Systems Manager tasks) are executed on managed nodes. You can define maintenance windows with specific schedules, durations, and targets to control when patching occurs and minimize operational impact.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/patch-manager.html

#### Imagebuilder Ssm Q20

When using Session Manager, which AWS service role provides the necessary permissions for SSM Agent to communicate with Systems Manager?

A. AmazonEC2RoleforSSM
B. AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
C. AWSServiceRoleForAmazonSSM
D. EC2InstanceProfileForSSM

**Answer: B.  AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore**

**Explanation:** AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore is the AWS managed policy that provides the minimum permissions required for EC2 instances to communicate with Systems Manager. It should be attached to the IAM instance profile associated with your EC2 instances to enable Session Manager functionality.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/session-manager-getting-started-instance-profile.html

### Incident Response Fundamentals

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q1

According to NIST 800-61, what are the four main phases of the incident response lifecycle?

A. Detection, Analysis, Containment, Recovery
B. Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, Post-Incident Activity
C. Planning, Execution, Monitoring, Improvement
D. Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond

**Answer: B.  Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, Post-Incident Activity**

**Explanation:** NIST 800-61 defines four phases: Preparation (getting ready before incidents), Detection & Analysis (identifying and understanding incidents), Containment/Eradication/Recovery (stopping, removing, and recovering from incidents), and Post-Incident Activity (learning and improving). AWS Security Incident Response aligns with this framework.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/aws-security-incident-response-guide.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q2

What is 'destination containment' in AWS incident response?

A. Blocking traffic at the source using AWS WAF rules and IP deny lists
B. Applying filtering or routing to prevent access to a targeted host or resource
C. Revoking IAM credentials associated with the compromised destination resource
D. Creating forensic snapshots of the destination system before isolation

**Answer: B.  Applying filtering or routing to prevent access to a targeted host or resource**

**Explanation:** Destination containment is applying filtering or routing within an environment to prevent access to a targeted host or resource. Examples include applying Network ACLs to block traffic, using isolation VPCs, detaching resources from Auto Scaling groups, and deregistering from load balancers.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/destination-containment.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q3

Which AWS service provides a managed incident response capability with 24/7 security experts?

A. Amazon GuardDuty
B. AWS Security Hub
C. AWS Security Incident Response
D. Amazon Detective

**Answer: C.  AWS Security Incident Response**

**Explanation:** AWS Security Incident Response is a managed service that provides 24/7 access to AWS security experts who help you prepare for, respond to, and recover from security events. It includes a self-service portal for case management and aligns with NIST 800-61.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/concepts-and-terminology.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q4

What is the first action you should take when you suspect an EC2 instance is compromised?

A. Immediately terminate the instance to stop the attacker and prevent lateral movement
B. Capture metadata and isolate the instance while preserving forensic evidence
C. Analyze CloudTrail logs to understand the scope before taking containment actions
D. Rotate the IAM role credentials attached to the instance to prevent API abuse

**Answer: B.  Capture metadata and isolate the instance while preserving forensic evidence**

**Explanation:** When responding to a potentially compromised EC2 instance, first capture metadata (instance ID, security groups, IAM role, etc.) and then isolate the instance while preserving evidence. This typically involves changing security groups to restrict traffic, taking EBS snapshots, and capturing memory if needed.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/operations.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q5

What is the purpose of an 'isolation VPC' in incident response?

A. A VPC with no internet gateway used to completely air-gap compromised instances
B. A pre-configured VPC to contain compromised resources while allowing legitimate AV/EDR traffic
C. A forensics VPC where EBS snapshots are restored for offline analysis
D. A staging VPC where instances are scanned before returning to production

**Answer: B.  A pre-configured VPC to contain compromised resources while allowing legitimate AV/EDR traffic**

**Explanation:** An isolation VPC is a pre-configured VPC that provides effective containment of potentially compromised resources while still allowing legitimate traffic (like antivirus or EDR solutions that need internet access). Resources are moved to this isolation VPC during active security events.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/destination-containment.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q6

How should you capture forensic evidence from an EC2 instance's EBS volume?

A. Use SSM Run Command to archive log files and upload them to an S3 bucket
B. Create an EBS snapshot immediately to preserve the complete disk state for analysis
C. Stop the instance and copy the volume to a forensics account using EBS copy
D. Create an AMI of the instance which captures both disk and memory state

**Answer: B.  Create an EBS snapshot immediately to preserve the complete disk state for analysis**

**Explanation:** Create EBS snapshots immediately to preserve the disk state for forensic analysis. Snapshots capture the entire volume at a point in time. You can then create new volumes from these snapshots in an isolated forensics environment for investigation without affecting the original evidence.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/operations.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q7

What is 'source containment' in AWS incident response?

A. Blocking the source of an attack from reaching AWS resources via IP blocks or credential revocation
B. Isolating the compromised destination resource from the rest of the network
C. Preserving the original evidence source before any forensic analysis begins
D. Identifying the origin of malicious traffic using VPC Flow Logs and CloudTrail

**Answer: A.  Blocking the source of an attack from reaching AWS resources via IP blocks or credential revocation**

**Explanation:** Source containment focuses on blocking the source of an attack from reaching AWS resources. This can include blocking IP addresses using security groups, NACLs, or AWS WAF; disabling compromised IAM credentials; or blocking specific users or roles that may be compromised.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/source-containment.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q8

What is the AWS Shared Responsibility Model's implication for incident response?

A. AWS handles all incident response activities
B. Customers handle all incident response activities
C. AWS secures the cloud infrastructure; customers are responsible for security in the cloud
D. Responsibility depends on the support plan tier

**Answer: C.  AWS secures the cloud infrastructure; customers are responsible for security in the cloud**

**Explanation:** Under the Shared Responsibility Model, AWS manages security OF the cloud (physical infrastructure, hypervisor, etc.), while customers are responsible for security IN the cloud (OS, applications, data, access management, etc.). For incident response, customers must prepare for and respond to incidents in their resources.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/introduction.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q9

What should be included in an incident response preparation plan?

A. Technical runbooks focused on automated remediation using Lambda and Step Functions
B. Contact lists, escalation procedures, runbooks, pre-provisioned access, and required tools
C. AWS account inventory with IAM policies and security group configurations documented
D. Network architecture diagrams showing VPC peering and Transit Gateway connections

**Answer: B.  Contact lists, escalation procedures, runbooks, pre-provisioned access, and required tools**

**Explanation:** Preparation should include: contact lists and escalation procedures, incident response runbooks, pre-provisioned access and tools, documented account and resource inventory, established relationships with AWS Support (if applicable), and regular testing through tabletop exercises and game days.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/preparation.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q10

How can you quickly isolate a potentially compromised EC2 instance from the network?

A. Terminate the instance to immediately stop all network activity and prevent further damage
B. Replace its security groups with a quarantine group that denies all inbound and outbound traffic
C. Modify the NACL associated with the subnet to block all traffic to the instance IP
D. Detach the IAM role to prevent the instance from making any AWS API calls

**Answer: B.  Replace its security groups with a quarantine group that denies all inbound and outbound traffic**

**Explanation:** The fastest way to network-isolate an EC2 instance is to replace its security groups with a 'quarantine' security group that has no inbound or outbound rules (denies all traffic by default). This preserves the instance for forensics while preventing further network communication.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/operations.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q11

What is the purpose of 'containment action preferences' in AWS Security Incident Response?

A. Configuration settings that define which AWS services are in scope for incident monitoring
B. Pre-authorized rapid response measures like isolating hosts and rotating credentials
C. Policies that specify which team members can access incident case information
D. Thresholds that trigger automatic escalation when security metrics exceed limits

**Answer: B.  Pre-authorized rapid response measures like isolating hosts and rotating credentials**

**Explanation:** Containment action preferences allow you to pre-authorize rapid response measures that the AWS Security Incident Response team can take during an active security event. This includes isolating compromised hosts, rotating credentials, and other containment actions to speed up response time.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/define-containment-preferences.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q12

What is 'triage' in the context of incident response?

A. The comprehensive post-incident report documenting root cause and lessons learned
B. The initial assessment and prioritization of a security event to determine response
C. The process of removing malware and closing vulnerabilities during eradication
D. The validation step confirming systems are clean before returning to production

**Answer: B.  The initial assessment and prioritization of a security event to determine response**

**Explanation:** Triage is the initial assessment and prioritization of a security event to determine the appropriate response and next steps. It involves quickly evaluating the severity, scope, and potential impact of an incident to allocate resources appropriately.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/concepts-and-terminology.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q13

What volatile data should be captured from a potentially compromised EC2 instance before isolation?

A. Instance metadata including security groups, IAM role, and network interface details
B. Memory contents, running processes, network connections, and logged-in users
C. EBS volume snapshots capturing the complete disk state for forensic analysis
D. CloudTrail logs and VPC Flow Logs related to the instance's recent API activity

**Answer: B.  Memory contents, running processes, network connections, and logged-in users**

**Explanation:** Volatile data (data lost when the instance is stopped) includes memory contents, running processes, network connections, logged-in users, and open files. This data should be captured before isolation or shutdown using memory acquisition tools if forensic analysis of runtime state is required.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/operations.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q14

How should Network ACLs be configured for destination containment?

A. Replace the existing NACL with a new one containing no rules for complete subnet isolation
B. Add explicit deny rules at the beginning of the NACL to block traffic to/from the target
C. Modify the default NACL rules to change from ALLOW to DENY for affected IP ranges
D. Associate a quarantine NACL that allows only management traffic from specific admin IPs

**Answer: B.  Add explicit deny rules at the beginning of the NACL to block traffic to/from the target**

**Explanation:** Network ACL rules are processed in top-down order. For destination containment, add explicit deny rules at the beginning of the NACL (lowest rule numbers) to block unauthorized traffic to/from the targeted resource. Alternatively, create a new NACL with only deny rules and associate it with the subnet.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/destination-containment.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q15

What is 'eradication' in the incident response lifecycle?

A. Isolating compromised resources from the network to prevent lateral movement
B. Removing the root cause and any artifacts or persistence mechanisms of the compromise
C. Restoring systems to normal operation after verifying they are clean
D. Documenting the incident timeline and creating a lessons learned report

**Answer: B.  Removing the root cause and any artifacts or persistence mechanisms of the compromise**

**Explanation:** Eradication involves removing the root cause of the incident and any artifacts left by the attacker. This includes removing malware, closing vulnerabilities that were exploited, removing unauthorized access, and ensuring the attacker no longer has persistence mechanisms.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/concepts-and-terminology.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q16

What AWS service provides automated forensic capabilities for EC2 instances?

A. AWS Config
B. Automated Forensics Orchestrator for Amazon EC2
C. Amazon Inspector
D. AWS Systems Manager

**Answer: B.  Automated Forensics Orchestrator for Amazon EC2**

**Explanation:** Automated Forensics Orchestrator for Amazon EC2 and EKS is an AWS Solution that provides a self-service framework for SOC teams to capture and examine data from EC2 instances and attached volumes for forensic analysis. It orchestrates key forensics processes including isolation of affected instances, capture of memory and disk images to secure storage, and initiation of automated investigation tools.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/solutions/latest/automated-forensics-orchestrator-for-amazon-ec2/welcome.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q17

What should be documented during post-incident activity?

A. A detailed timeline of events with timestamps for each containment action taken
B. Lessons learned, root cause analysis, and specific improvements to prevent recurrence
C. Names and roles of all responders along with their individual actions during the incident
D. Financial impact assessment including remediation costs and business disruption estimates

**Answer: B.  Lessons learned, root cause analysis, and specific improvements to prevent recurrence**

**Explanation:** Post-incident activity should document: timeline of events, actions taken, root cause analysis, lessons learned, and recommended improvements. This information feeds back into the preparation phase to improve future incident response capabilities.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/post-incident-activity.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q18

Why should you detach compromised EC2 instances from Auto Scaling groups during containment?

A. To stop the instance from receiving traffic through the load balancer immediately
B. To prevent the Auto Scaling group from terminating the instance and destroying evidence
C. To allow the security team to modify the instance without triggering scaling policies
D. To reduce the blast radius by preventing the compromise from spreading to new instances

**Answer: B.  To prevent the Auto Scaling group from terminating the instance and destroying evidence**

**Explanation:** You should detach compromised instances from Auto Scaling groups to prevent the group from terminating the instance (destroying forensic evidence) or launching replacement instances that might also be compromised. This also prevents the affected instance from serving traffic.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/destination-containment.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q19

What is 'Responder Generated Intelligence' in AWS Security Incident Response?

A. Automated threat reports generated by GuardDuty using machine learning analysis
B. Indicators of compromise, TTPs, and patterns observed during AWS investigations
C. Log analysis insights produced by Amazon Detective's behavioral graph
D. Security findings aggregated and prioritized by Security Hub's scoring algorithm

**Answer: B.  Indicators of compromise, TTPs, and patterns observed during AWS investigations**

**Explanation:** Responder Generated Intelligence includes indicators of compromise (IOCs), tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), and associated patterns observed by AWS during investigations. This intelligence helps identify and respond to evolving security threats.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/concepts-and-terminology.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q20

What is the recommended approach for handling compromised IAM credentials?

A. Monitor CloudTrail logs closely to understand attacker behavior before taking action
B. Immediately deactivate the credentials and review CloudTrail for recent unauthorized actions
C. Rotate the credentials to new values while keeping the existing ones temporarily active
D. Apply a restrictive IAM policy to the user that limits permissions to read-only access

**Answer: B.  Immediately deactivate the credentials and review CloudTrail for recent unauthorized actions**

**Explanation:** When IAM credentials are compromised, immediately deactivate or delete the affected credentials (access keys, passwords). Then review CloudTrail logs to understand what actions were taken with those credentials, and assess the blast radius of the compromise.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/operations.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q21

What is the purpose of 'game days' in incident response preparation?

A. Tabletop exercises where teams discuss hypothetical scenarios without hands-on action
B. Simulated security incidents to practice response procedures in a realistic environment
C. Annual security awareness training required for compliance with industry regulations
D. Authorized penetration testing engagements to identify vulnerabilities before attackers

**Answer: B.  Simulated security incidents to practice response procedures in a realistic environment**

**Explanation:** Game days are simulated security incidents that help teams practice their incident response procedures in a controlled environment. They help identify gaps in runbooks, test communication channels, and ensure responders are familiar with tools and processes before a real incident occurs.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/preparation.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q22

How should you preserve evidence chain of custody in AWS?

A. Store EBS snapshots and logs in the same account with versioning enabled for rollback
B. Document all access to evidence and store forensic artifacts in separate restricted accounts
C. Use CloudTrail to automatically track all API calls made during the investigation
D. Enable S3 Object Lock on all buckets to prevent modification of stored evidence

**Answer: B.  Document all access to evidence and store forensic artifacts in separate restricted accounts**

**Explanation:** Maintain chain of custody by: documenting all access to evidence (who, when, what), storing forensic artifacts (snapshots, logs) in a separate, restricted account, using write-once storage for logs, enabling MFA delete, and using cryptographic hashes to verify integrity.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/operations.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q23

What happens when you stop an EC2 instance for forensics?

A. Both preserve all data identically since EBS volumes persist through either action
B. Stopping loses volatile data like memory but preserves EBS volumes for disk forensics
C. Stopping triggers a clean OS shutdown preserving more filesystem state than terminating
D. Stopping is preferred because it allows the instance to be restarted for live analysis

**Answer: B.  Stopping loses volatile data like memory but preserves EBS volumes for disk forensics**

**Explanation:** Stopping an EC2 instance (normal stop) loses volatile data (memory, running processes) but preserves EBS volumes. For forensics, if you need volatile data, you must capture it before stopping. Stopping is often preferred to preserve disk evidence while preventing further network activity. Note: In AWS EC2, 'stopping' is the standard action; 'shutting down' typically refers to the OS-level shutdown command which results in the instance stopping.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/destination-containment.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q24

What should you review in CloudTrail when investigating a security incident?

A. Failed API calls which indicate blocked attacker activity and permission errors
B. All relevant API calls including source IPs, user agents, timestamps, and affected resources
C. Management events only since data events are too voluminous for incident investigation
D. Events from the detection time window to limit the scope of investigation

**Answer: B.  All relevant API calls including source IPs, user agents, timestamps, and affected resources**

**Explanation:** During investigation, review all relevant CloudTrail events including: API calls by the suspected compromised identity, source IP addresses, user agents, affected resources, timestamps, and both successful and failed attempts. This helps establish the timeline and scope of the incident.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-security-incident-response-guide/operations.html

#### Incident Response Fundamentals Q25

What is the role of AWS Support during a security incident?

A. AWS Support is only available for infrastructure issues, not customer security incidents
B. Business or Enterprise Support provides guidance with Enterprise including TAM and expert access
C. AWS Support proactively monitors and automatically remediates security threats in your account
D. AWS Support provides incident response only through the separately purchased Security Hub service

**Answer: B.  Business or Enterprise Support provides guidance with Enterprise including TAM and expert access**

**Explanation:** AWS Business and Enterprise Support customers can receive guidance during security incidents. Enterprise Support includes access to a Technical Account Manager (TAM) and, with the AWS Security Incident Response service, 24/7 access to security experts for active incident support.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/security-ir/latest/userguide/concepts-and-terminology.html

### Inspector

#### Inspector Q1

What is Amazon Inspector primarily designed to do?

A. Monitor network traffic in real-time
B. Continuously scan workloads for software vulnerabilities and network exposure
C. Perform penetration testing on AWS infrastructure
D. Audit IAM permissions and policies

**Answer: B.  Continuously scan workloads for software vulnerabilities and network exposure**

**Explanation:** Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability management service that automatically discovers workloads and continuously scans them for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. It scans EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/what-is-inspector.html

#### Inspector Q2

Which resource types does Amazon Inspector scan? (Choose the most complete answer)

A. Only EC2 instances
B. EC2 instances and ECR container images
C. EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions
D. All AWS compute resources including ECS tasks

**Answer: C.  EC2 instances, ECR container images, and Lambda functions**

**Explanation:** Amazon Inspector discovers and scans three resource types: Amazon EC2 instances, container images in Amazon ECR, and AWS Lambda functions. It does not scan ECS tasks directly (only their underlying ECR images).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/what-is-inspector.html

#### Inspector Q3

What are the two scan methods Amazon Inspector uses for EC2 instances?

A. Deep scan and surface scan
B. Agent-based scanning and agentless scanning
C. Network scanning and vulnerability scanning
D. Active scanning and passive scanning

**Answer: B.  Agent-based scanning and agentless scanning**

**Explanation:** Amazon Inspector uses two scan methods for EC2 instances: agent-based scanning (using SSM agent to collect software inventory) and agentless scanning (using EBS snapshots). By default, hybrid scanning mode uses both methods.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-ec2.html

#### Inspector Q4

What is the default scanning mode when you first activate Amazon Inspector?

A. Agent-based only
B. Agentless only
C. Hybrid scanning (both agent-based and agentless)
D. Manual scanning

**Answer: C.  Hybrid scanning (both agent-based and agentless)**

**Explanation:** When you activate Amazon Inspector for the first time, your account is automatically enrolled in hybrid scanning mode, which uses both agent-based and agentless scan methods for EC2 instances. You can change this setting at any time.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-ec2.html

#### Inspector Q5

What AWS service does agent-based scanning require to be installed on EC2 instances?

A. CloudWatch agent
B. SSM Agent (Systems Manager agent)
C. Inspector agent
D. CloudTrail agent

**Answer: B.  SSM Agent (Systems Manager agent)**

**Explanation:** Agent-based scanning requires the SSM Agent (AWS Systems Manager agent) to be installed and running on EC2 instances. Amazon Inspector uses SSM associations to collect software inventory. The SSM Agent is pre-installed on many Amazon Machine Images (AMIs).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-ec2.html#agent-based

#### Inspector Q6

How does agentless scanning collect software inventory from EC2 instances?

A. By reading CloudWatch Logs
B. By taking and analyzing EBS snapshots
C. By querying the EC2 API
D. By installing a temporary agent

**Answer: B.  By taking and analyzing EBS snapshots**

**Explanation:** Agentless scanning collects software inventory by creating and analyzing Amazon EBS snapshots of EC2 instances. This method doesn't require any agent to be installed on the instance, making it useful for instances where the SSM agent cannot be installed.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-ec2.html#agentless

#### Inspector Q7

What are the three finding states in Amazon Inspector?

A. Open, In Progress, Closed
B. Active, Suppressed, Closed
C. New, Acknowledged, Resolved
D. Critical, High, Low

**Answer: B.  Active, Suppressed, Closed**

**Explanation:** Amazon Inspector categorizes findings in three states: Active (not remediated), Suppressed (subject to suppression rules), and Closed (remediated). When a finding is remediated, Inspector automatically detects it and closes the finding.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/findings-understanding.html

#### Inspector Q8

What is the Amazon Inspector Risk Score?

A. A fixed CVSS score from the NVD database
B. A contextualized score that adjusts the NVD base score based on your environment
C. A compliance score from 0-100
D. A custom score you set manually

**Answer: B.  A contextualized score that adjusts the NVD base score based on your environment**

**Explanation:** The Amazon Inspector Risk Score is a contextualized severity score that adjusts the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) base CVSS score according to your specific environment. For example, it may lower the score if a network vulnerability exists but there's no open network path to the internet.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/what-is-inspector.html

#### Inspector Q9

How long does Amazon Inspector retain closed findings before deleting them?

A. Immediately after closing
B. 3 days for terminated resources, 30 days for other reasons
C. 90 days for all findings
D. Indefinitely

**Answer: B.  3 days for terminated resources, 30 days for other reasons**

**Explanation:** When a resource is deleted or terminated, Inspector automatically closes findings and deletes them after 3 days. If findings are closed for any other reason (like remediation), they are deleted after 30 days. This allows time for auditing and verification.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/findings-understanding.html

#### Inspector Q10

What service does Amazon Inspector integrate with to publish findings as events?

A. CloudWatch Events
B. Amazon EventBridge
C. Amazon SNS directly
D. AWS Step Functions

**Answer: B.  Amazon EventBridge**

**Explanation:** Amazon Inspector publishes findings to Amazon EventBridge as finding events. EventBridge can then route these findings to targets like Lambda functions, SNS topics, or SQS queues, enabling automated remediation workflows and notifications.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/findings-managing-automating-responses.html

#### Inspector Q11

How can you centrally manage Amazon Inspector across multiple AWS accounts?

A. Use IAM cross-account roles
B. Designate a delegated administrator account through AWS Organizations
C. Create a master-slave configuration
D. Use CloudFormation StackSets

**Answer: B.  Designate a delegated administrator account through AWS Organizations**

**Explanation:** If your environment uses AWS Organizations, you can designate a delegated administrator account for Amazon Inspector. This account can activate Inspector for the entire organization with a single click, view aggregated findings, and manage scans for all member accounts.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/what-is-inspector.html

#### Inspector Q12

What happens when Amazon Inspector detects that a vulnerability has been remediated?

A. You must manually close the finding
B. Inspector automatically closes the finding
C. The finding moves to 'under review' status
D. Inspector sends a notification but keeps the finding open

**Answer: B.  Inspector automatically closes the finding**

**Explanation:** Amazon Inspector automatically detects when a finding has been appropriately remediated and closes it automatically. If the issue reoccurs within seven days, Inspector will reopen the finding.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/what-is-inspector.html

#### Inspector Q13

When does Amazon Inspector rescan EC2 instances for vulnerabilities?

A. Only when you manually trigger a scan
B. When new instances launch, when software is installed, or when new CVEs are published
C. Every 24 hours on a fixed schedule
D. Only during maintenance windows

**Answer: B.  When new instances launch, when software is installed, or when new CVEs are published**

**Explanation:** Amazon Inspector continuously scans and initiates new vulnerability scans when: (1) you launch a new EC2 instance, (2) you install new software on an existing instance, or (3) Amazon Inspector adds a new CVE to its database that's relevant to your instance.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-ec2.html#agent-based

#### Inspector Q14

What is Lambda code scanning in Amazon Inspector?

A. Scanning Lambda function logs for errors
B. Scanning Lambda IAM roles and permissions
C. An optional layer that scans application code and dependencies for CVEs
D. Scanning Lambda network configurations

**Answer: C.  An optional layer that scans application code and dependencies for CVEs**

**Explanation:** Lambda code scanning is an optional scan type that evaluates application package dependencies used in Lambda functions for CVEs. It leverages the Amazon Q Developer scanning engine to scan first-party application code, third-party dependencies, and Infrastructure as Code.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-resources.html

#### Inspector Q15

How does Amazon Inspector handle ECR container image scanning?

A. Only scans images pushed in the last 7 days
B. Converts repositories to enhanced scanning and scans images pushed or pulled recently
C. Requires manual initiation of each scan
D. Only scans official AWS images

**Answer: B.  Converts repositories to enhanced scanning and scans images pushed or pulled recently**

**Explanation:** When you activate Amazon ECR scanning, Inspector converts all repositories from basic to enhanced scanning. It scans all active images pushed/activated in the last 30 days or pulled within the last 90 days, and continues monitoring images for 90 days by default.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-resources.html

#### Inspector Q16

What IAM managed policy provides the minimum permissions needed for EC2 instances to work with Amazon Inspector agent-based scanning?

A. AmazonInspector2FullAccess
B. AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
C. AmazonEC2ReadOnlyAccess
D. AWSSecurityHubServiceRolePolicy

**Answer: B.  AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore**

**Explanation:** The AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy is the recommended IAM policy to attach to EC2 instance profiles for agent-based scanning. It provides all the permissions needed for the SSM agent to function and for Amazon Inspector to collect software inventory.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-ec2.html#agent-based

#### Inspector Q17

What are suppression rules in Amazon Inspector?

A. Rules that prevent Inspector from scanning specific resources
B. Rules that hide unwanted findings from your views without deleting them
C. Rules that automatically remediate findings
D. Rules that suppress notifications to Security Hub

**Answer: B.  Rules that hide unwanted findings from your views without deleting them**

**Explanation:** Suppression rules allow you to filter and hide unwanted findings from your findings list without deleting them. Findings subject to suppression rules are categorized as 'Suppressed' and don't appear in your active findings views or reports.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/findings-managing-supression-rules.html

#### Inspector Q18

Which service-linked roles does Amazon Inspector create when activated?

A. AWSServiceRoleForInspector only
B. AWSServiceRoleForAmazonInspector2 and AWSServiceRoleForAmazonInspector2Agentless
C. AWSServiceRoleForSecurityHub
D. No service-linked roles are created

**Answer: B.  AWSServiceRoleForAmazonInspector2 and AWSServiceRoleForAmazonInspector2Agentless**

**Explanation:** Amazon Inspector creates two service-linked roles: AWSServiceRoleForAmazonInspector2 (for agent-based scanning and general operations) and AWSServiceRoleForAmazonInspector2Agentless (for agentless scanning operations). These roles allow Inspector to access required AWS services.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/getting_started.html

#### Inspector Q19

How frequently does Amazon Inspector perform network reachability scans on EC2 instances?

A. Continuously in real-time
B. Once every 12 hours
C. Once per day
D. Only when instance configuration changes

**Answer: B.  Once every 12 hours**

**Explanation:** Amazon Inspector performs network reachability scans once every 12 hours to detect unintended network exposure. Package vulnerability scans are performed on a variable cadence depending on the scan method (agent-based scans more frequently when changes occur).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/scanning-ec2.html

#### Inspector Q20

What happens to Amazon Inspector findings if you deactivate Inspector?

A. Findings are permanently archived
B. Findings are removed after 24 hours
C. Findings are retained indefinitely
D. Findings are immediately deleted

**Answer: B.  Findings are removed after 24 hours**

**Explanation:** If you disable Amazon Inspector, all findings are removed after 24 hours. For terminated resources, findings are removed after 3 days. If AWS suspends your account, findings are removed after 90 days. This is important to consider before deactivating the service.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/inspector/latest/user/findings-understanding.html

### Kms

#### Kms Q1

An application uses SSE-S3 for S3 encryption. The security team asks what type of KMS key is being used. What should you tell them?

A. A customer managed key created automatically in your account by the S3 service
B. An AWS managed key (aws/s3) that appears in your KMS console and is managed by S3
C. An AWS owned key managed by AWS across multiple customer accounts, not visible in your console
D. No KMS key is used; SSE-S3 uses S3-specific encryption that bypasses KMS entirely

**Answer: D.  No KMS key is used; SSE-S3 uses S3-specific encryption that bypasses KMS entirely**

**Explanation:** SSE-S3 does NOT use KMS at all. S3 manages encryption keys entirely internally using AES-256, separate from the KMS service. If you need KMS features (CloudTrail key usage logging, key policies, customer managed keys), you must use SSE-KMS instead. The aws/s3 AWS managed key only appears when using SSE-KMS, not SSE-S3.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingServerSideEncryption.html

#### Kms Q2

A developer tries to encrypt a 10 KB file using the KMS Encrypt API directly and receives an error. Why?

A. The Encrypt API requires the file to be base64 encoded first, doubling the effective size limit
B. The Encrypt API has a 4 KB limit; use GenerateDataKey for envelope encryption of larger data
C. The Encrypt API only works with text data; binary files require the EncryptBinary API instead
D. The Encrypt API requires a specific encryption context that wasn't provided with the request

**Answer: B.  The Encrypt API has a 4 KB limit; use GenerateDataKey for envelope encryption of larger data**

**Explanation:** KMS can only directly encrypt up to 4 KB of data with the Encrypt API. For larger data, use envelope encryption: GenerateDataKey to get a data key, encrypt your data locally with that key, then store the encrypted data key alongside.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/APIReference/API_Encrypt.html

#### Kms Q3

An architect describes their encryption approach: 'Generate a data key, use its plaintext to encrypt our files locally, then store the encrypted data key with the ciphertext.' What is this called?

A. Key wrapping - where the data key wraps around the encrypted data for protection
B. Envelope encryption - using a data key for data and a KMS key to protect the data key
C. Hierarchical encryption - creating a key hierarchy with the KMS key at the root
D. Dual encryption - encrypting both the key and data separately for defense in depth

**Answer: B.  Envelope encryption - using a data key for data and a KMS key to protect the data key**

**Explanation:** Envelope encryption uses a two-tier approach: A data key encrypts your actual data locally (fast, unlimited size), then KMS encrypts that data key with your KMS key (never exceeds 4 KB). Store the encrypted data key with your ciphertext.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/concepts.html#enveloping

#### Kms Q4

An application stores encrypted data keys for batch processing later. It doesn't need to encrypt data immediately when generating the keys. Which API should it use?

A. GenerateDataKey with a flag to suppress the plaintext key from the response
B. GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext to receive only the encrypted data key
C. GenerateDataKey followed immediately by shredding the plaintext from memory
D. CreateDataKey with delayed activation to prevent immediate plaintext access

**Answer: B.  GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext to receive only the encrypted data key**

**Explanation:** GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext returns only the encrypted data key, not the plaintext. Use this when you need to store the key for later but don't need to encrypt immediately. Call Decrypt when you're ready to use the key.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/APIReference/API_GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext.html

#### Kms Q5

A compliance auditor asks how often KMS automatically rotates customer managed symmetric keys when rotation is enabled. What is the interval?

A. Every 90 days (quarterly) to align with common compliance frameworks
B. Every 180 days (semi-annually) as a balance between security and operational overhead
C. Every 365 days (annually), with old key material retained for decryption
D. The rotation interval is configurable from 30 to 365 days based on security requirements

**Answer: C.  Every 365 days (annually), with old key material retained for decryption**

**Explanation:** Automatic key rotation for customer managed symmetric keys occurs every 365 days (1 year). KMS creates new cryptographic material but retains ALL previous versions indefinitely, ensuring you can always decrypt old data.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html

#### Kms Q6

A security engineer configures IAM policies to grant kms:Encrypt to a role. The role still can't encrypt with the target KMS key. What might be missing?

A. The role also needs kms:GenerateDataKey permission for the encryption to work
B. The KMS key policy must also allow the role access; IAM alone is insufficient for KMS
C. The role needs to be in the same account as the KMS key for IAM policies to work
D. The KMS key must have a key alias configured before IAM policies can reference it

**Answer: B.  The KMS key policy must also allow the role access; IAM alone is insufficient for KMS**

**Explanation:** KMS requires key policies for access. Unlike most AWS services, IAM policies ALONE cannot grant KMS access. The key policy must either allow the specific principal OR allow IAM policies to grant permissions (via the 'Enable IAM policies' statement).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policies.html

#### Kms Q7

A security team needs to give an external contractor's IAM role temporary access to decrypt data with a KMS key for a 2-week audit. They don't want to modify the key policy or create permanent IAM policies. What mechanism should be used?

A. Add the contractor's role ARN to the key policy and remove it after the audit
B. Create a KMS grant for the contractor's IAM role with Decrypt permission
C. Share the key with the contractor's AWS account using Resource Access Manager (RAM)
D. Create temporary IAM credentials for the contractor with an expiration date

**Answer: B.  Create a KMS grant for the contractor's IAM role with Decrypt permission**

**Explanation:** KMS grants provide temporary, delegated access to specific KMS operations without modifying key policies or IAM policies. Grants can be created for any IAM principal (users, roles) and retired when no longer needed. This is ideal for time-limited access like audits or contractor engagements.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/grants.html

#### Kms Q8

An S3 bucket uses SSE-KMS with encryption context {'bucket': 'prod-data', 'purpose': 'analytics'}. A Lambda tries to decrypt an object but doesn't specify encryption context. What happens?

A. Decryption succeeds but the encryption context is logged as empty in CloudTrail
B. Decryption fails because the encryption context must match exactly for successful decryption
C. Decryption succeeds because encryption context is optional metadata not enforced cryptographically
D. Decryption fails with an access denied error rather than a decryption error

**Answer: B.  Decryption fails because the encryption context must match exactly for successful decryption**

**Explanation:** Encryption context is cryptographically bound to the ciphertext as additional authenticated data (AAD). You MUST provide the exact same encryption context for decryption - it's not optional metadata but a security control.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/concepts.html#encrypt_context

#### Kms Q9

A KMS key was accidentally scheduled for deletion 5 days ago (waiting period is 7 days). Can the data encrypted with this key still be recovered?

A. No, once deletion is scheduled, the key is immediately disabled and data is unrecoverable
B. Yes, cancel the deletion within the waiting period and the key will be restored to active state
C. Yes, but only by contacting AWS Support to restore the key before the waiting period expires
D. No, but AWS automatically backs up key material so data can be recovered after deletion

**Answer: B.  Yes, cancel the deletion within the waiting period and the key will be restored to active state**

**Explanation:** During the waiting period (7-30 days), the key is disabled but can be recovered by canceling the deletion. Once the waiting period expires, the key and all data encrypted with it become PERMANENTLY unrecoverable - there are no backups.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/deleting-keys.html

#### Kms Q10

A regulated company must maintain physical control of their HSMs for compliance. They also want to use KMS APIs. What should they implement?

A. AWS CloudHSM in single-tenant mode with custom KMS integration through API Gateway
B. A Custom Key Store that backs KMS keys with an AWS CloudHSM cluster they control
C. On-premises HSM with AWS Direct Connect and custom key import for each KMS operation
D. AWS Outposts with dedicated KMS hardware deployed in their data center

**Answer: B.  A Custom Key Store that backs KMS keys with an AWS CloudHSM cluster they control**

**Explanation:** A Custom Key Store lets you back KMS keys with an AWS CloudHSM cluster that you control. This provides KMS convenience (APIs, integration) with CloudHSM's dedicated, single-tenant HSMs. Keys never leave the HSM in plaintext.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/custom-key-store-overview.html

#### Kms Q11

A company has key material generated by their on-premises HSM and wants to use it in KMS for regulatory reasons. Which approach is correct?

A. Create an AWS managed key and contact AWS Support to upload the key material
B. Create a customer managed key with 'External' origin and import the key material
C. Create any KMS key and use the ReEncrypt API to transfer the key material from the HSM
D. Create a Custom Key Store and synchronize key material from the on-premises HSM

**Answer: B.  Create a customer managed key with 'External' origin and import the key material**

**Explanation:** You can import your own key material into customer managed KMS keys by creating a key with 'External' origin. This gives you control over key generation but note: imported keys don't support automatic rotation and you can set an expiration date.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys.html

#### Kms Q12

A partner without AWS access needs to send encrypted data that only your application can decrypt. The partner cannot call AWS APIs. Which approach enables this?

A. Create a symmetric KMS key and share the key material with the partner for local encryption
B. Create an asymmetric KMS key and share the downloadable public key with the partner for encryption
C. Create a symmetric KMS key and have the partner use envelope encryption with a shared secret
D. Create an asymmetric KMS key and share the private key with the partner for encryption

**Answer: B.  Create an asymmetric KMS key and share the downloadable public key with the partner for encryption**

**Explanation:** Asymmetric KMS keys have a public/private key pair. You can download the public key and share it with external parties who don't have AWS access. They encrypt data with the public key (outside AWS), and your application decrypts with the private key via KMS. The private key never leaves KMS.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/symmetric-asymmetric.html

#### Kms Q13

An architect needs to create an asymmetric KMS key for both document signing and message encryption. How should they proceed?

A. Create one asymmetric key and specify both SIGN_VERIFY and ENCRYPT_DECRYPT as key usages
B. Create two separate asymmetric keys: one for signing and one for encryption
C. Create one asymmetric key for signing; use a symmetric key for encryption instead
D. Create one asymmetric key for encryption; use AWS Certificate Manager for signing

**Answer: B.  Create two separate asymmetric keys: one for signing and one for encryption**

**Explanation:** An asymmetric KMS key can perform EITHER signing/verification OR encryption/decryption, but NOT both. You must create separate keys for each purpose. This enforces separation of duties and follows cryptographic best practices.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/symmetric-asymmetric.html

#### Kms Q14

A security team wants a KMS key to only be usable when called through S3 (not directly via KMS APIs). Which condition key enforces this?

A. kms:CallerService with StringEquals condition matching 's3.amazonaws.com'
B. kms:ViaService with StringEquals condition matching 's3.region.amazonaws.com'
C. aws:SourceService with StringEquals condition matching 's3.amazonaws.com'
D. kms:EncryptionContext with a required key identifying S3 as the caller

**Answer: B.  kms:ViaService with StringEquals condition matching 's3.region.amazonaws.com'**

**Explanation:** kms:ViaService restricts key usage to requests from specific AWS services. The format is 'servicename.region.amazonaws.com' (e.g., s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com). This prevents direct KMS API calls while allowing S3 operations.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/policy-conditions.html#conditions-kms-via-service

#### Kms Q15

A global application needs data encrypted in us-east-1 to be decryptable in eu-west-1 without cross-region API calls. What KMS feature should they use?

A. Cross-region key replication that automatically copies the key to all enabled regions
B. Multi-Region keys that share key material and can decrypt each other's ciphertext
C. Global KMS keys that are accessible from all regions through a global endpoint
D. Key aliases that point to different regional keys with synchronized key material

**Answer: B.  Multi-Region keys that share key material and can decrypt each other's ciphertext**

**Explanation:** Multi-Region keys are interoperable KMS keys in different regions with the same key material. Data encrypted in one region can be decrypted in another using the related multi-Region key, without cross-region calls. Useful for DR and global apps.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/multi-region-keys-overview.html

#### Kms Q16

A new KMS key is created without specifying a custom key policy. The key creator's IAM role doesn't have any KMS permissions in its identity policy. Can they use the key?

A. No, the creator must explicitly grant themselves permissions in the key policy
B. Yes, the default policy allows the root user full access and enables IAM policy permissions
C. Yes, the key creator automatically gets all permissions through an implicit creator policy
D. No, but AWS Support can grant initial access if the creator is locked out

**Answer: B.  Yes, the default policy allows the root user full access and enables IAM policy permissions**

**Explanation:** The default key policy allows the AWS account (root user) full access and enables IAM policies to grant permissions. This prevents lockout and allows flexible permission management. The creator doesn't automatically get permissions unless granted.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/key-policies.html#key-policy-default

#### Kms Q17

An application references KMS keys by ARN. A key needs to be rotated manually to new key material. How can this be done without updating the application?

A. Enable automatic rotation which replaces the key ARN transparently
B. Use a key alias; update the alias to point to the new key without changing the ARN reference
C. Import new key material into the existing key, which doesn't change the key ID or ARN
D. Create the new key with the same key ID as the old key to maintain the same ARN

**Answer: B.  Use a key alias; update the alias to point to the new key without changing the ARN reference**

**Explanation:** Key aliases are friendly names (alias/my-key) that point to KMS keys. Update the alias to point to a different key without changing application code. Note: if using ARNs directly, you'd need to update to use alias ARNs instead.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/kms-alias.html

#### Kms Q18

A security team needs to audit all uses of a specific KMS key, including what data was associated with each encryption. What should they review?

A. KMS key metrics in CloudWatch, which include encryption context as a dimension
B. CloudTrail logs, which record all KMS API calls including encryption context
C. AWS Config rules that track KMS key usage and associated resource configurations
D. KMS access logs in S3, similar to S3 server access logging for buckets

**Answer: B.  CloudTrail logs, which record all KMS API calls including encryption context**

**Explanation:** KMS logs ALL API calls to CloudTrail, including key ID, encryption context (if provided), caller identity, and timestamps. Encryption context is visible in logs (it's not secret), making it invaluable for audit trails.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html

#### Kms Q19

An AWS service receives a KMS grant to use a key. The security team wants to ensure the service can only operate on resources with a specific tag. What grant feature enables this?

A. Grant constraints with tag conditions specifying required resource tags
B. Grant constraints requiring specific encryption context that includes the tag value
C. Grant scope that limits operations to resources matching a tag-based ARN pattern
D. Grant policies that attach IAM-style tag conditions to the grant permissions

**Answer: B.  Grant constraints requiring specific encryption context that includes the tag value**

**Explanation:** Grant constraints like EncryptionContextEquals require specific encryption context values for operations. By requiring the tag value in the encryption context, you ensure operations only work for properly tagged resources (assuming the tag is included in context).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/grant-manage.html

#### Kms Q20

A customer managed KMS key has automatic rotation disabled. The security team wants to enable it. What must they verify first?

A. The key must have at least one key alias configured before rotation can be enabled
B. The key must use KMS-generated key material, not imported key material
C. The key must have been created within the last 365 days to support rotation
D. The key must be in the same region as the primary CloudTrail trail for audit logging

**Answer: B.  The key must use KMS-generated key material, not imported key material**

**Explanation:** Automatic rotation is only supported for symmetric keys with KMS-generated key material. Imported key material, asymmetric keys, keys in Custom Key Stores, and HMAC keys don't support automatic rotation - you must rotate them manually.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html#rotating-keys-enable-disable

#### Kms Q21

An application needs to migrate encrypted data from one KMS key to another without ever exposing plaintext to the application. Which API should be used?

A. Decrypt with the old key then Encrypt with the new key in a single atomic transaction
B. ReEncrypt to decrypt under the source key and re-encrypt under the destination key within KMS
C. GenerateDataKey with the new key to create new data keys for re-encryption
D. CopyEncryptedData API that handles key migration transparently in KMS

**Answer: B.  ReEncrypt to decrypt under the source key and re-encrypt under the destination key within KMS**

**Explanation:** ReEncrypt decrypts ciphertext under one key and re-encrypts it under another key entirely within KMS. The plaintext is never exposed to the caller, making it ideal for key migration or changing encryption contexts securely.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/APIReference/API_ReEncrypt.html

#### Kms Q22

An administrator schedules a KMS key for deletion with a 7-day waiting period. On day 4, they realize the key is still needed. What can they do?

A. Nothing - once scheduled, deletion cannot be canceled and the key is already disabled
B. Contact AWS Support to expedite restoration before the 7-day period expires
C. Cancel the scheduled deletion; the key returns to disabled state and can be re-enabled
D. Restore the key from the automatic backup that KMS creates before scheduling deletion

**Answer: C.  Cancel the scheduled deletion; the key returns to disabled state and can be re-enabled**

**Explanation:** During the waiting period (7-30 days), you can cancel deletion. The key returns to disabled state - you must explicitly enable it to use it again. After the waiting period, deletion is permanent with no recovery option.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/deleting-keys.html

#### Kms Q23

A key policy allows cross-account access to Account B. The security team wants to restrict access to only specific roles in Account B. Which condition key helps?

A. kms:PrincipalOrgID to verify the caller is in the same AWS Organization
B. kms:CallerAccount combined with aws:PrincipalArn to restrict to specific roles in that account
C. kms:CrossAccountAccess to enable fine-grained cross-account permission controls
D. aws:SourceAccount to verify which account is making the KMS API request

**Answer: B.  kms:CallerAccount combined with aws:PrincipalArn to restrict to specific roles in that account**

**Explanation:** Use kms:CallerAccount to verify the caller's account, and combine with aws:PrincipalArn conditions to restrict to specific roles. This provides fine-grained cross-account access control beyond just allowing the entire account.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/policy-conditions.html#conditions-kms-caller-account

#### Kms Q24

A partner needs to encrypt data that only your AWS application can decrypt. They don't have AWS access. How can this be achieved with KMS?

A. Share your KMS key ID with them so they can call the KMS Encrypt API directly
B. Create an asymmetric key and give them the downloadable public key for encryption
C. Create a symmetric key and export the key material for them to use locally
D. Set up a VPN connection so they can securely access your KMS endpoint

**Answer: B.  Create an asymmetric key and give them the downloadable public key for encryption**

**Explanation:** You can download the public key of an asymmetric KMS key and share it with external parties. They encrypt data with the public key (no AWS access needed), and you decrypt with the private key via KMS (never leaves KMS).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/download-public-key.html

#### Kms Q25

An application needs to ensure message integrity without encryption. The messages should be verified as authentic and unmodified. Which KMS key type should be used?

A. Symmetric encryption key with encryption context containing a hash of the message
B. Asymmetric signing key to sign messages and distribute the public key for verification
C. HMAC key to generate and verify message authentication codes for integrity
D. Any KMS key type works since all encryption implicitly provides integrity verification

**Answer: C.  HMAC key to generate and verify message authentication codes for integrity**

**Explanation:** KMS HMAC keys generate and verify Hash-based Message Authentication Codes. They ensure message integrity and authenticity without encryption. Both GenerateMac and VerifyMac happen entirely within KMS. Asymmetric signing would also work but HMAC is simpler for this use case.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/hmac.html

### Kms Imported Keys Xks

#### Kms Imported Keys Xks Q1

What is the common term for importing your own key material into AWS KMS?

A. Bring Your Own Key (BYOK), which allows you to supply your own key material to AWS KMS
B. External Key Management (EKM), which manages keys outside AWS and imports them for cryptographic operations
C. Customer Managed Encryption (CME), which provides full control over key generation and rotation policies
D. Self-Provided Keys (SPK), which enables organizations to maintain copies of encryption keys externally

**Answer: A.  Bring Your Own Key (BYOK), which allows you to supply your own key material to AWS KMS**

**Explanation:** Importing key material into AWS KMS is commonly known as 'Bring Your Own Key' (BYOK). This feature allows you to generate key material using your own entropy source and import it into KMS keys, while KMS handles the lifecycle management within AWS.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys.html

#### Kms Imported Keys Xks Q2

Which types of KMS keys support imported key material?

A. Only symmetric encryption KMS keys support imported key material for backward compatibility with legacy systems
B. Symmetric encryption keys, asymmetric keys (except ML-DSA), HMAC keys, and multi-Region keys of supported types
C. All KMS key types including keys in custom key stores like CloudHSM and external key stores
D. Symmetric and asymmetric keys but not HMAC keys or multi-Region keys due to implementation constraints

**Answer: B.  Symmetric encryption keys, asymmetric keys (except ML-DSA), HMAC keys, and multi-Region keys of supported types**

**Explanation:** AWS KMS supports imported key material for symmetric encryption keys, asymmetric keys (except ML-DSA keys), HMAC keys, and multi-Region keys of all supported types. However, you CANNOT import key material into KMS keys in custom key stores (CloudHSM or External Key Stores).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys.html

#### Kms Imported Keys Xks Q3

What is the key origin value for a KMS key designed to use imported key material?

A. IMPORTED indicating the key material was provided by the customer rather than generated by AWS KMS
B. EXTERNAL indicating the key material comes from outside AWS KMS and is managed by the customer
C. CUSTOMER_PROVIDED indicating the customer supplied the key material through the import process
D. BYOK indicating this is a bring-your-own-key implementation with customer-managed key material

**Answer: B.  EXTERNAL indicating the key material comes from outside AWS KMS and is managed by the customer**

**Explanation:** KMS keys designed for imported key material have an origin value of EXTERNAL. This origin value is permanent and cannot be changed. You cannot convert a KMS key with AWS KMS-generated key material (origin: AWS_KMS) into one designed for imported key material, or vice versa.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys-considerations.html

#### Kms Imported Keys Xks Q4

Can you enable automatic key rotation for a KMS key with imported key material?

A. Yes, automatic rotation is supported but requires reimporting the same key material every 365 days
B. No, automatic rotation is not supported, but you can perform manual rotation or on-demand rotation for symmetric keys
C. Yes, but only for symmetric encryption keys and not for asymmetric or HMAC keys with imported material
D. No, rotation requires generating new key material which AWS KMS cannot do for imported keys

**Answer: B.  No, automatic rotation is not supported, but you can perform manual rotation or on-demand rotation for symmetric keys**

**Explanation:** Automatic key rotation is NOT supported for KMS keys with imported key material because AWS KMS cannot generate new key material for these keys. However, you can manually rotate keys by creating a new KMS key with new imported material. For symmetric encryption keys with imported material, you can use on-demand rotation to import multiple key materials.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys-considerations.html

#### Kms Imported Keys Xks Q5

What happens when you delete imported key material from a KMS key?

A. The KMS key enters a 7-30 day waiting period before permanent deletion, allowing you to cancel if needed
B. The key material is deleted immediately with no recovery option, rendering the KMS key unusable for operations
C. The key material moves to a quarantine state for 24 hours before permanent deletion as a safety measure
D. The KMS key reverts to AWS-managed key material generation and continues functioning with new material

**Answer: B.  The key material is deleted immediately with no recovery option, rendering the KMS key unusable for operations**

**Explanation:** When you delete imported key material, AWS KMS deletes it IMMEDIATELY with no recovery option from AWS. The KMS key becomes unusable for cryptographic operations. This is different from scheduling KMS key deletion (7-30 day waiting period). To make the key usable again, you must reimport the same key material.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys-considerations.html

#### Kms Imported Keys Xks Q6

Can you set an expiration time for imported key material?

A. Yes, and when the expiration time arrives AWS KMS automatically reimports the material if you provided backup copies
B. Yes, and when the expiration time arrives AWS KMS deletes the key material rendering the KMS key unusable
C. No, expiration times are only supported for AWS-generated key material to ensure consistent key lifecycle management
D. No, but you can configure CloudWatch alarms that trigger Lambda functions to delete expired imported materials

**Answer: B.  Yes, and when the expiration time arrives AWS KMS deletes the key material rendering the KMS key unusable**

**Explanation:** Yes, when you import key material, you can set an expiration time. When the expiration arrives, AWS KMS automatically deletes the key material, making the KMS key unusable. To restore it, you must reimport the same key material. You can create CloudWatch alarms to notify you before expiration occurs.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys-considerations.html

#### Kms Imported Keys Xks Q7

Who is responsible for the availability and durability of imported key material?

A. AWS KMS maintains the same availability and durability guarantees as AWS-generated keys through redundant storage
B. The customer is responsible; AWS KMS does not maintain imported key material at the same durability level
C. Shared responsibility: AWS maintains availability while customers ensure durability through external backup copies
D. AWS KMS for availability during active use; customers for durability if key material expires or is deleted

**Answer: B.  The customer is responsible; AWS KMS does not maintain imported key material at the same durability level**

**Explanation:** The customer is responsible for the availability and durability of imported key material. AWS KMS keeps imported material highly available while in use, but does NOT maintain it at the same durability level as AWS-generated keys. You must maintain external copies of your imported key material to reimport if deleted or expired.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys-considerations.html

#### Kms Imported Keys Xks Q8

Can you export key material that you previously imported into AWS KMS?

A. Yes, using the ExportKeyMaterial API with proper IAM permissions and MFA authentication enabled
B. No, AWS KMS cannot return imported key material in any form; you must maintain external copies
C. Yes, but only within 30 days of import and only to the AWS account that performed the import
D. No, unless you encrypted the original import using a customer-managed KMS key that still exists

**Answer: B.  No, AWS KMS cannot return imported key material in any form; you must maintain external copies**

**Explanation:** You CANNOT export any key material that you imported into AWS KMS. AWS KMS cannot return the imported key material to you in any form. This is why you must maintain a copy of your imported key material outside of AWS (preferably in an HSM or key manager) so you can reimport it if needed.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys-considerations.html

#### Kms Imported Keys Xks Q9

For asymmetric and HMAC keys with imported key material, can you import different key material into the same KMS key?

A. Yes, you can import different key material to perform key rotation and maintain backward compatibility
B. No, the KMS key is permanently associated with the original imported key material for these key types
C. Yes, but only once every 90 days to prevent confusion and ensure proper key management practices
D. No, unless you first delete the KMS key and recreate it with a new key ID and policy

**Answer: B.  No, the KMS key is permanently associated with the original imported key material for these key types**

**Explanation:** For asymmetric and HMAC keys, when you import key material, the KMS key is PERMANENTLY associated with that key material. You can reimport the SAME key material, but you cannot import DIFFERENT key material into that KMS key. Only symmetric encryption keys support importing multiple different key materials for on-demand rotation.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys-considerations.html

#### Kms Imported Keys Xks Q10

What advanced rotation capability do symmetric encryption keys with imported key material support?

A. Automatic annual rotation that generates new key material within AWS KMS HSMs without customer intervention
