They help improve code maintainability and follow best practices but don't represent security vulnerabilities or functional issues.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/code-issue-severity.html

#### Qdeveloper Codeguru Q23

How can developers initiate an Amazon Q Developer code review for an entire repository?

A. Only through the AWS console by uploading a zip file
B. Open the repository in the IDE and enter 'Review my repository' in the Q chat panel
C. Configure automatic daily scans in AWS CodeBuild
D. Use the AWS CLI command 'aws q review-repository'

**Answer: B.  Open the repository in the IDE and enter 'Review my repository' in the Q chat panel**

**Explanation:** To review an entire repository (not just changes), open the repository in your IDE and enter natural language commands like 'Review my repository' in the Amazon Q chat panel. If you just say 'Review my code', Q will attempt to review only code changes by default. You must explicitly ask for a full repository review.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/start-review.html

#### Qdeveloper Codeguru Q24

What infrastructure as code (IaC) security issues can Amazon Q Developer detect?

A. Only CloudFormation syntax errors
B. Misconfigurations, compliance issues, and security problems in IaC files
C. Only Terraform state file corruption
D. IaC performance optimization opportunities

**Answer: B.  Misconfigurations, compliance issues, and security problems in IaC files**

**Explanation:** Amazon Q can review Infrastructure as Code (IaC) files to detect misconfigurations, compliance violations, and security issues. This includes checking for insecure default configurations, overly permissive security groups, unencrypted resources, and other security best practice violations in IaC templates before infrastructure is deployed.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/code-reviews.html

#### Qdeveloper Codeguru Q25

What is the maximum source code size (after filtering) that Amazon Q Developer can scan in project reviews?

A. 10 MB
B. 50 MB
C. 100 MB
D. 200 MB

**Answer: B.  50 MB**

**Explanation:** For file or project reviews, Amazon Q Developer can scan up to 50 MB of source code after filtering out third-party libraries and unsupported files. The total input artifact size can be up to 500 MB (including all files, libraries, build artifacts). For auto reviews, both limits are much lower at 200 KB to ensure real-time performance.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazonq/latest/qdeveloper-ug/code-reviews.html

### Ram Wellarchitected

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q1

What is the primary purpose of AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)?

A. To provide identity federation and single sign-on access for users across multiple AWS accounts in an organization
B. To securely share AWS resources across accounts, organizations, and OUs without duplicating resources in each account
C. To manage resource quotas and service limits centrally across all accounts in an AWS Organizations hierarchy
D. To automate resource provisioning using infrastructure-as-code templates deployed across multiple AWS accounts simultaneously

**Answer: B.  To securely share AWS resources across accounts, organizations, and OUs without duplicating resources in each account**

**Explanation:** AWS RAM enables secure sharing of AWS resources across accounts within your organization or with external accounts. This eliminates the need to provision duplicate resources in every account, reducing operational overhead while maintaining security through managed permissions.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/what-is.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q2

Before using AWS RAM to share resources within an AWS Organization, which prerequisite must be completed?

A. Enable AWS Config recording in all member accounts and configure aggregators in the management account
B. Enable resource sharing with AWS Organizations from the management account using the RAM console or CLI
C. Deploy AWS CloudFormation StackSets to all member accounts with the AWSRAMServiceRolePolicy attached
D. Configure cross-account IAM roles in each member account with trust relationships to the management account

**Answer: B.  Enable resource sharing with AWS Organizations from the management account using the RAM console or CLI**

**Explanation:** You must enable sharing with AWS Organizations from the organization's management account using the RAM console or the enable-sharing-with-aws-organization CLI command. This creates the AWSServiceRoleForResourceAccessManager service-linked role. The organization must also have all features enabled.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/getting-started-sharing.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q3

A company wants to share a VPC subnet with specific member accounts in their organization. Which principals can be specified when creating the resource share?

A. Individual AWS account IDs, entire AWS Organizations, organizational units (OUs), or IAM roles and users within the sharing account
B. Individual AWS account IDs, entire AWS Organizations, organizational units (OUs), or cross-account IAM roles with explicit trust policies
C. Only individual AWS account IDs or entire AWS Organizations; OU-level sharing requires AWS Control Tower integration
D. Only IAM principals (roles and users) within the same AWS account; cross-account sharing requires VPC peering

**Answer: A.  Individual AWS account IDs, entire AWS Organizations, organizational units (OUs), or IAM roles and users within the sharing account**

**Explanation:** AWS RAM allows sharing with individual account IDs (inside or outside your organization), entire organizations, OUs, or IAM roles/users (for resource types that support this). For VPC subnets, you can share with accounts, organizations, or OUs, but not with individual IAM roles/users.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/getting-started-sharing.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q4

When sharing resources within an AWS Organization using RAM, what happens when a principal receives a resource share?

A. The principal receives an email invitation that must be explicitly accepted before accessing the shared resources
B. The principal automatically gains access to shared resources without exchanging invitations or manual acceptance
C. The principal must request access through AWS Service Catalog and receive approval from the resource owner
D. The principal receives a notification in AWS Security Hub that requires acknowledgment within 7 days

**Answer: B.  The principal automatically gains access to shared resources without exchanging invitations or manual acceptance**

**Explanation:** When sharing resources within an AWS Organization, RAM does not send invitations. Principals in your organization automatically gain access to shared resources. Invitations are only sent when sharing with accounts outside your organization.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/getting-started-sharing.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q5

Which statement correctly describes how AWS RAM handles permissions for shared resources?

A. RAM automatically grants full administrative permissions to all principals specified in the resource share
B. RAM uses AWS managed permissions or customer managed permissions to define what actions principals can perform on shared resources
C. RAM requires resource owners to manually create IAM policies in each consumer account for accessing shared resources
D. RAM relies on resource-based policies attached directly to each resource; managed permissions are not supported

**Answer: B.  RAM uses AWS managed permissions or customer managed permissions to define what actions principals can perform on shared resources**

**Explanation:** AWS RAM uses managed permissions (AWS-managed or customer-managed) to control what actions principals can perform on shared resources. These permissions are applied consistently across all consumers of the share, ensuring security and reducing management overhead.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/what-is.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q6

A security team wants to centrally share an AWS Transit Gateway with 50 accounts in their organization. What is the benefit of using RAM instead of manually configuring access in each account?

A. RAM automatically replicates the Transit Gateway to each account's region for lower latency connectivity
B. RAM creates a single resource that appears natively in all consumer accounts without duplication or manual configuration
C. RAM establishes VPN tunnels between accounts that provide encrypted communication through the Transit Gateway
D. RAM converts the Transit Gateway into a managed service that AWS operates and maintains for all accounts

**Answer: B.  RAM creates a single resource that appears natively in all consumer accounts without duplication or manual configuration**

**Explanation:** When you share a Transit Gateway using RAM, the single resource appears natively in all consumer accounts' consoles and API results. Users see it as if it were directly in their account, eliminating the need to create duplicate resources or manually configure access in each account.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/what-is.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q7

Which AWS resource types support sharing with individual IAM roles and users within the same account?

A. All resource types supported by RAM can be shared with IAM roles and users for fine-grained access control
B. Only a subset of resource types (like App Mesh meshes, License Manager configurations, and specific database resources) support IAM-level sharing
C. None; RAM only supports sharing at the account level, not with individual IAM principals
D. Only resource types that have resource-based policies can be shared with IAM roles and users

**Answer: B.  Only a subset of resource types (like App Mesh meshes, License Manager configurations, and specific database resources) support IAM-level sharing**

**Explanation:** Only specific resource types support sharing with IAM roles and users. Most resources can only be shared at the account level. Check the shareable resources documentation to see which types support IAM-level sharing (indicated by 'Yes' in the 'Can share with IAM users and roles' column).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/shareable.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q8

What happens if a consumer account leaves an AWS Organization after receiving shared resources through RAM?

A. The consumer account retains permanent access to the shared resources regardless of organization membership
B. The consumer account loses access to all resources shared within the organization but retains access to external shares
C. The shared resources are automatically replicated to the departing account before access is revoked
D. The resource owner receives a notification but must manually revoke access using IAM policies

**Answer: B.  The consumer account loses access to all resources shared within the organization but retains access to external shares**

**Explanation:** When sharing with AWS Organizations is enabled, resource sharing is restricted to consumers within the same organization. If a consumer leaves the organization, they automatically lose access to resources shared within that organization. This applies whether shared with OUs, the entire organization, or individual accounts.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/getting-started-sharing.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q9

A company shares an Amazon Aurora database cluster using RAM with external accounts. What must external account principals do to access the shared resource?

A. Accept the resource share invitation sent to their email address and configure VPC peering to the owner's VPC
B. Accept the resource share invitation through the RAM console or CLI before they can access the shared resource
C. Request access through AWS Service Catalog and wait for the resource owner to provision access credentials
D. No action required; external accounts automatically receive read-only access to shared resources

**Answer: B.  Accept the resource share invitation through the RAM console or CLI before they can access the shared resource**

**Explanation:** When sharing with accounts outside your organization, RAM sends invitations that must be explicitly accepted. The consumer account must accept the invitation through the RAM console or CLI before they can access the shared resource. This provides control over which external accounts can use your resources.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/working-with-shared.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q10

Which statement accurately describes AWS RAM's integration with AWS CloudTrail?

A. CloudTrail logs only resource share creation and deletion events; individual resource access is not logged
B. CloudTrail logs all RAM API calls including resource share management and provides visibility into resource usage by consumers
C. CloudTrail integration requires a separate AWS Config recorder to be enabled in each participating account
D. CloudTrail logs are only available in the resource owner's account; consumer accounts cannot audit their resource usage

**Answer: B.  CloudTrail logs all RAM API calls including resource share management and provides visibility into resource usage by consumers**

**Explanation:** AWS RAM integrates with CloudTrail to log all RAM API calls, including creating, modifying, and deleting resource shares, as well as accepting/rejecting invitations. This provides comprehensive visibility and auditability for shared resources across accounts.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/what-is.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q11

What is the difference between sharing resources with RAM versus using resource-based policies?

A. Resource-based policies provide better security through fine-grained IAM permissions while RAM only supports account-level access
B. RAM provides native service console visibility, supports OU/organization sharing, and shows resource owners which principals access resources
C. Resource-based policies support cross-region sharing while RAM is limited to resources within a single AWS region
D. RAM requires AWS Organizations while resource-based policies work with standalone accounts outside any organization

**Answer: B.  RAM provides native service console visibility, supports OU/organization sharing, and shows resource owners which principals access resources**

**Explanation:** While resource-based policies can share some resources, RAM provides additional benefits: 1) Shared resources appear natively in consumer consoles/APIs, 2) You can share with entire organizations or OUs without enumerating accounts, 3) Resource owners can see which principals access their resources. RAM provides a consistent experience across resource types.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ram/latest/userguide/what-is.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q12

What is AWS Well-Architected Tool used for?

A. To automatically remediate security findings and compliance violations detected by AWS Config and Security Hub
B. To measure workloads against AWS best practices using lenses and provide recommendations for improving architecture
C. To perform penetration testing and vulnerability assessments on deployed AWS resources across multiple accounts
D. To generate cost optimization reports by analyzing resource utilization patterns and recommending rightsizing actions

**Answer: B.  To measure workloads against AWS best practices using lenses and provide recommendations for improving architecture**

**Explanation:** AWS Well-Architected Tool helps you measure your workloads against AWS best practices defined in the Well-Architected Framework. It assists with documenting architecture decisions, provides recommendations for improvement, and guides you in making workloads more reliable, secure, efficient, and cost-effective.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/intro.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q13

In AWS Well-Architected Tool, what is a workload?

A. A collection of AWS accounts managed by AWS Organizations that share common security and compliance requirements
B. A collection of resources and code that delivers business value, spanning single or multiple AWS accounts
C. An automated deployment pipeline using AWS CodePipeline that provisions infrastructure across development and production environments
D. A CloudFormation stack or set of related stacks that deploy a complete application with all necessary resources

**Answer: B.  A collection of resources and code that delivers business value, spanning single or multiple AWS accounts**

**Explanation:** In the Well-Architected Tool context, a workload is a collection of resources and code that delivers business value, such as a customer-facing application or backend process. It can consist of resources in a single account or span multiple accounts. A workload can range from a small subset to thousands of resources.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/workloads.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q14

Which lens is automatically applied when defining a new workload in AWS Well-Architected Tool?

A. The Security Pillar Lens, which focuses exclusively on security best practices across all six pillars
B. The AWS Well-Architected Framework Lens, which covers all six pillars of the Well-Architected Framework
C. The Serverless Applications Lens, which is recommended for all modern cloud-native architectures
D. The Cost Optimization Lens, which helps identify opportunities to reduce AWS spending

**Answer: B.  The AWS Well-Architected Framework Lens, which covers all six pillars of the Well-Architected Framework**

**Explanation:** The AWS Well-Architected Framework Lens is automatically applied when a workload is defined. This lens covers all six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability. Additional lenses from the Lens Catalog or custom lenses can be added as needed.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/lenses.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q15

What are the two types of lenses available in AWS Well-Architected Tool?

A. Mandatory lenses that must be applied to all workloads, and optional lenses that can be selectively applied
B. Lens Catalog lenses created by AWS, and custom lenses created by users with their own best practices
C. Foundation lenses for general workloads, and specialized lenses for specific industries like healthcare or finance
D. Public lenses shared across all AWS accounts, and private lenses restricted to specific AWS Organizations

**Answer: B.  Lens Catalog lenses created by AWS, and custom lenses created by users with their own best practices**

**Explanation:** AWS Well-Architected Tool supports two types of lenses: 1) Lens Catalog lenses - official lenses created and maintained by AWS (like Serverless, SaaS, Container Build), and 2) Custom lenses - user-defined lenses with custom pillars, questions, and best practices that can be shared with other AWS accounts.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/lenses.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q16

How many lenses can be applied to a single workload in AWS Well-Architected Tool?

A. A maximum of 5 lenses can be added at one time, with an overall limit of 20 lenses per workload
B. An unlimited number of lenses can be applied to accommodate complex workloads with diverse requirements
C. Only one lens can be active at a time; switching lenses requires creating a new workload definition
D. A maximum of 3 lenses: the mandatory Well-Architected Framework lens plus 2 additional lenses

**Answer: A.  A maximum of 5 lenses can be added at one time, with an overall limit of 20 lenses per workload**

**Explanation:** Five lenses can be added at a time to a workload, with a maximum of 20 lenses applied to one workload overall. This allows you to assess your workload against multiple perspectives while maintaining manageable review processes.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/lenses.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q17

What happens to lens data when a lens is removed from a workload?

A. All data associated with the lens is permanently deleted and cannot be recovered
B. The data is retained; if you add the lens back to the workload, the data is restored
C. The data is archived to S3 Glacier and can be retrieved after a 12-hour restoration period
D. The data is converted to a read-only format and exported as a PDF report

**Answer: B.  The data is retained; if you add the lens back to the workload, the data is restored**

**Explanation:** When a lens is removed from a workload, the data associated with that lens is retained. If you add the lens back to the workload later, all the previous data is restored, allowing you to continue from where you left off without losing your review progress.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/lenses.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q18

What are High Risk Issues (HRIs) and Medium Risk Issues (MRIs) in AWS Well-Architected Tool?

A. HRIs are security vulnerabilities requiring immediate patching; MRIs are compliance gaps requiring documentation
B. HRIs are architectural choices that might significantly negatively impact business; MRIs have lesser but still notable impact
C. HRIs are AWS service outages affecting workload availability; MRIs are performance degradations impacting user experience
D. HRIs are cost overruns exceeding budget by more than 50%; MRIs are overruns between 20-50%

**Answer: B.  HRIs are architectural choices that might significantly negatively impact business; MRIs have lesser but still notable impact**

**Explanation:** High Risk Issues (HRIs) are architectural and operational choices AWS has found might significantly negatively impact business operations, assets, or individuals. Medium Risk Issues (MRIs) also might negatively impact business, but to a lesser extent. These are identified based on your responses to Well-Architected review questions.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/workloads.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q19

How can workloads be shared in AWS Well-Architected Tool?

A. Workloads can only be viewed by the AWS account that created them; sharing requires exporting to PDF
B. Workloads can be shared with other AWS accounts, IAM users, AWS Organizations, or organizational units (OUs)
C. Workloads can be shared through AWS Service Catalog by publishing them as approved products
D. Workloads can be shared using AWS RAM to grant read-only access to specific resource shares

**Answer: B.  Workloads can be shared with other AWS accounts, IAM users, AWS Organizations, or organizational units (OUs)**

**Explanation:** AWS Well-Architected Tool allows you to share workloads with other AWS accounts, IAM users within your account, entire AWS Organizations, or specific organizational units (OUs). This enables collaboration on architecture reviews across teams and accounts.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/workloads.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q20

What information does the Workloads page display for each workload?

A. Current monthly costs, projected annual costs, and cost optimization opportunities identified by AWS Cost Explorer
B. Name, owner, questions answered, high/medium risk count, improvement status, and last updated timestamp
C. Compliance status against SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, and other regulatory frameworks with evidence artifacts
D. Resource inventory, security group configurations, IAM policy analysis, and encryption status across all services

**Answer: B.  Name, owner, questions answered, high/medium risk count, improvement status, and last updated timestamp**

**Explanation:** The Workloads page displays: workload name, owner (AWS account ID), number of questions answered, count of high risk issues (HRIs), count of medium risk issues (MRIs), improvement status (None/Not Started/In Progress/Complete/Risk Acknowledged), and last updated date/time.

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q21

Which AWS service integration helps you answer Well-Architected Tool review questions more easily?

A. AWS Config provides resource configuration history that helps answer infrastructure design questions
B. AWS Trusted Advisor and AWS Service Catalog AppRegistry help discover information needed for review questions
C. AWS CloudFormation templates and AWS CDK code can be automatically analyzed to generate review answers
D. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store provides centralized documentation that populates question responses

**Answer: B.  AWS Trusted Advisor and AWS Service Catalog AppRegistry help discover information needed for review questions**

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q22

Who are the intended users of AWS Well-Architected Tool?

A. Exclusively AWS Solutions Architects and AWS Enterprise Support account managers
B. Technical product development teams including CTOs, architects, developers, and operations personnel
C. Only Chief Security Officers (CSOs) and compliance officers responsible for audit and governance
D. AWS Marketplace sellers who need to certify their solutions meet AWS architectural standards

**Answer: B.  Technical product development teams including CTOs, architects, developers, and operations personnel**

It helps document architectures, provide product launch governance, and manage risks in technology portfolios.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/userguide/intro.html

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q23

What happens when a workload is deleted in AWS Well-Architected Tool?

A. The workload is moved to a 30-day recycle bin where it can be restored before permanent deletion
B. The workload and all associated milestones are permanently deleted and cannot be undone
C. The workload is archived to S3 and can be restored within 90 days using the AWS CLI
D. Only the owner can delete the workload; shared users can only remove their own access

**Answer: B.  The workload and all associated milestones are permanently deleted and cannot be undone**

#### Ram Wellarchitected Q24

How can an organization use custom lenses in AWS Well-Architected Tool?

B. Custom lenses allow organizations to create their own pillars, questions, and best practices tailored to specific needs
C. Custom lenses are pre-built industry templates that AWS provides for regulated sectors like healthcare and finance
D. Custom lenses automatically generate compliance reports for SOC 2, ISO 27001, and other certification audits

These can be tailored to specific technologies or help meet governance needs within the organization. #### Ram Wellarchitected Q25

What is the improvement status feature used for in AWS Well-Architected Tool?

B. To manually track the progress of implementing improvements: None, Not Started, In Progress, Complete, or Risk Acknowledged

### Rcp Declarative Policies

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q1

What is the primary purpose of Resource Control Policies (RCPs) in AWS Organizations?

A. To restrict the maximum available permissions for IAM principals (users and roles) within your organization's member accounts
B. To restrict IAM principals external to your organization from accessing resources within your organization's member accounts
C. To automate the creation of IAM roles across multiple accounts with consistent permission sets
D. To enforce encryption requirements on resources across all accounts using service-specific policies

**Answer: B.  To restrict IAM principals external to your organization from accessing resources within your organization's member accounts**

**Explanation:** RCPs are resource-centric controls that restrict external principals from accessing your resources. Use SCPs to control what your internal principals can do, and RCPs to control who can access your resources. RCPs help build a data perimeter around your organization.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q2

Which AWS services currently support Resource Control Policies (RCPs)?

A. All AWS services that support resource-based policies including IAM, EC2, Lambda, and RDS
B. S3, STS, KMS, SQS, Secrets Manager, Cognito, CloudWatch Logs, DynamoDB, ECR, and OpenSearch Serverless
C. Only services with cross-account access capabilities such as S3, Lambda, SNS, and SQS
D. EC2, VPC, IAM, CloudFormation, and Systems Manager for infrastructure security enforcement

**Answer: B.  S3, STS, KMS, SQS, Secrets Manager, Cognito, CloudWatch Logs, DynamoDB, ECR, and OpenSearch Serverless**

**Explanation:** RCPs currently support a specific subset of AWS services: S3, STS, KMS, SQS, Secrets Manager, Cognito, CloudWatch Logs, DynamoDB, ECR, and OpenSearch Serverless. RCP support is being expanded over time. Check documentation for the current list.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q3

Do Resource Control Policies (RCPs) affect resources in the management account?

A. Yes, RCPs apply uniformly to all accounts including the management account for consistent governance
B. No, RCPs do not affect resources in the management account, only member accounts including delegated administrators
C. Yes, but only if explicitly enabled through a special RCP attachment process for the management account
D. No, unless the management account is explicitly included in the RCP target list via ARN specification

**Answer: B.  No, RCPs do not affect resources in the management account, only member accounts including delegated administrators**

**Explanation:** RCPs do not affect resources in the management account. They only affect resources in member accounts (including delegated administrator accounts). This is an important limitation to understand when designing your data perimeter strategy.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q4

What is the key distinction between how SCPs and RCPs are applied in AWS Organizations?

A. SCPs are principal-centric controls limiting what your identities can do; RCPs are resource-centric controls limiting who can access your resources
B. SCPs block API actions before execution; RCPs validate resource configurations after resources are created
C. SCPs apply to the management account; RCPs apply only to member accounts in the organization
D. SCPs use Allow statements; RCPs use Deny statements to define access restrictions

**Answer: A.  SCPs are principal-centric controls limiting what your identities can do; RCPs are resource-centric controls limiting who can access your resources**

**Explanation:** SCPs control what principals in your organization can do (principal-centric). RCPs control who can access resources in your organization (resource-centric). Together, they create a data perimeter protecting both identities and resources.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_authorization_policies.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q5

When enabling RCPs in your organization, what AWS managed policy is automatically attached?

A. RCPDefaultPolicy that denies all external access until explicit Allow statements are added
B. RCPFullAWSAccess that allows all access to pass through RCP evaluation until you create custom RCPs
C. RCPExternalAccessDeny that blocks all principals outside your organization by default
D. RCPOrganizationOnly that restricts access to principals within your AWS Organizations structure

**Answer: B.  RCPFullAWSAccess that allows all access to pass through RCP evaluation until you create custom RCPs**

**Explanation:** When you enable RCPs, the RCPFullAWSAccess AWS managed policy is automatically attached to the root, all OUs, and all accounts. This policy allows all access to pass through RCP evaluation. You cannot detach this policy. It ensures existing permissions continue working until you add restrictive RCPs.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps_evaluation.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q6

How do Deny statements in RCPs propagate through the organizational hierarchy?

A. Deny statements at higher levels are inherited by child OUs and accounts but can be overridden with explicit Allow statements
B. A Deny statement at any level in the path from root to account blocks access; no inheritance overrides are possible
C. Deny statements only apply to the specific OU or account they are attached to and do not affect children
D. Deny statements require unanimous agreement across all levels in the hierarchy to take effect

**Answer: B.  A Deny statement at any level in the path from root to account blocks access; no inheritance overrides are possible**

**Explanation:** For a permission to be denied for a resource, ANY RCP from the root through each OU to the target account can deny that permission. Deny statements are powerful and cannot be overridden. Test carefully before attaching RCPs to the root.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps_evaluation.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q7

What is the primary purpose of Declarative Policies in AWS Organizations?

A. To declare and enforce access control rules for IAM principals across organizational accounts
B. To centrally declare and enforce desired configuration for AWS services, maintaining baseline settings even when services add new features
C. To declare compliance requirements and automatically remediate non-compliant resources using Lambda functions
D. To define resource tagging requirements and enforce consistent tag application across the organization

**Answer: B.  To centrally declare and enforce desired configuration for AWS services, maintaining baseline settings even when services add new features**

**Explanation:** Declarative policies allow you to centrally declare and enforce your desired configuration for AWS services at scale. The key benefit is 'set once and forget' - the baseline configuration is maintained even when services introduce new features or APIs.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q8

Where are declarative policies enforced, and how does this differ from authorization policies?

A. Declarative policies are enforced at the AWS CloudTrail level; authorization policies are enforced at the IAM level
B. Declarative policies are enforced in the service's control plane; authorization policies regulate access to APIs
C. Declarative policies are enforced by AWS Config rules; authorization policies are enforced by service control policies
D. Declarative policies are enforced at the VPC network boundary; authorization policies are enforced at resource endpoints

**Answer: B.  Declarative policies are enforced in the service's control plane; authorization policies regulate access to APIs**

**Explanation:** Declarative policies are enforced directly in the service's control plane (not at the API level). This ensures the baseline configuration is always enforced, even when new features or APIs are introduced. Authorization policies (SCPs/RCPs) regulate API access.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q9

Can declarative policies govern service-linked roles?

A. No, service-linked roles are exempt from all organizational policies including declarative policies
B. Yes, declarative policies can govern service-linked roles unlike SCPs and RCPs which cannot
C. Yes, but only if the service-linked role is explicitly specified in the declarative policy document
D. No, service-linked roles must be managed through AWS Support escalations and cannot be governed by policies

**Answer: B.  Yes, declarative policies can govern service-linked roles unlike SCPs and RCPs which cannot**

**Explanation:** Declarative policies CAN govern service-linked roles, which is a key distinction from SCPs and RCPs. This is because declarative policies are enforced at the service control plane level, not the API authorization level.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q10

What feature do declarative policies offer that SCPs and RCPs do not?

A. Automatic remediation of non-compliant resources using AWS Systems Manager Automation documents
B. Customizable error messages that can include URLs to internal wiki pages or compliance documentation
C. Cross-region policy replication ensuring consistent enforcement in all AWS regions simultaneously
D. Real-time alerting to Security Hub when configuration drift is detected across accounts

**Answer: B.  Customizable error messages that can include URLs to internal wiki pages or compliance documentation**

**Explanation:** Declarative policies allow custom error messages. When an action fails due to a declarative policy, you can set the error message or provide a custom URL. SCPs and RCPs provide non-customizable 'access denied' errors.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q11

Which EC2-related configurations can be controlled using declarative policies?

A. EC2 instance types allowed for launch, maximum number of instances per account, and EBS volume size limits
B. VPC Block Public Access, Serial Console Access, Image Block Public Access, Allowed Images, Instance Metadata Defaults, and Snapshot Block Public Access
C. Security group rule requirements, network ACL configurations, and VPC subnet CIDR range restrictions
D. EC2 Auto Scaling policies, Elastic Load Balancer configurations, and CloudWatch alarm thresholds

**Answer: B.  VPC Block Public Access, Serial Console Access, Image Block Public Access, Allowed Images, Instance Metadata Defaults, and Snapshot Block Public Access**

**Explanation:** Declarative policies for EC2 support: VPC Block Public Access (internet gateway controls), Serial Console Access, Image Block Public Access (AMI sharing), Allowed Images Settings, Instance Metadata Defaults (IMDSv2 enforcement), and Snapshot Block Public Access.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative_syntax.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q12

What happens to resource configurations when a declarative policy is detached?

A. Resources maintain their current configuration until manually changed; the policy no longer enforces future changes
B. The attribute state rolls back to its previous state before the declarative policy was attached
C. Resources enter a pending state and require administrator approval to continue operating
D. AWS Config automatically remediates resources to the default AWS configuration for the service

**Answer: B.  The attribute state rolls back to its previous state before the declarative policy was attached**

**Explanation:** When a declarative policy is detached, the attribute state rolls back to its previous state before the policy was attached. This allows for testing and reversibility of declarative policy enforcement.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q13

What is the purpose of the Account Status Report for declarative policies?

A. To track account billing status and identify accounts with overdue payments requiring policy suspension
B. To review the current status of all attributes supported by declarative policies, identifying uniform and inconsistent configurations across accounts
C. To audit IAM user access patterns and identify unused credentials for security hardening
D. To monitor account health metrics including API throttling rates and service quota utilization

**Answer: B.  To review the current status of all attributes supported by declarative policies, identifying uniform and inconsistent configurations across accounts**

**Explanation:** The Account Status Report shows the current status of all declarative policy attributes for accounts in scope. It identifies uniform configurations (all accounts match) versus inconsistent configurations, and displays the most frequent value. This helps assess readiness before applying policies.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q14

For VPC Block Public Access declarative policy, what are the two modes for internet_gateway_block?

A. block_all that prevents all internet traffic, and block_untrusted that allows only whitelisted IPs
B. block_ingress that blocks inbound internet traffic except NAT/EGRESS gateways, and block_bidirectional that blocks all traffic except excluded VPCs
C. block_public that prevents public IP association, and block_routing that prevents route table modifications
D. block_external that denies cross-account access, and block_regional that restricts traffic to same region only

**Answer: B.  block_ingress that blocks inbound internet traffic except NAT/EGRESS gateways, and block_bidirectional that blocks all traffic except excluded VPCs**

**Explanation:** VPC Block Public Access modes: block_ingress (blocks internet traffic to VPCs except NAT/EGRESS gateways which only allow outbound), and block_bidirectional (blocks all traffic to/from internet gateways and EGRESS gateways except excluded VPCs/subnets).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative_syntax.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q15

What is the difference between creating VPC Block Public Access exclusions via declarative policy versus in the account?

A. Declarative policies create permanent exclusions; account-level exclusions are temporary and require monthly renewal
B. Declarative policies can only configure if exclusions are allowed (enabled/disabled); actual exclusions must be created in the account owning the VPC
C. Declarative policies create regional exclusions; account-level exclusions apply globally across all regions
D. Declarative policies require AWS Organizations admin role; account-level exclusions can be created by any IAM user

**Answer: B.  Declarative policies can only configure if exclusions are allowed (enabled/disabled); actual exclusions must be created in the account owning the VPC**

**Explanation:** The declarative policy attribute configures whether exclusions are allowed (enabled/disabled), but you cannot create the actual exclusions in the policy. Exclusions must be created in the account that owns the VPC.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative_syntax.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q16

What does the Image Block Public Access declarative policy control?

A. Blocks launching EC2 instances from AMIs that do not have encryption enabled for all EBS volumes
B. Blocks sharing AMIs publicly or cross-account except through approved AWS Resource Access Manager shares
C. Prevents public AMI sharing while allowing cross-account sharing; blocks public snapshot sharing except for verified accounts
D. Prevents creation of AMIs from running instances that have public IP addresses assigned

**Answer: C.  Prevents public AMI sharing while allowing cross-account sharing; blocks public snapshot sharing except for verified accounts**

**Explanation:** Image Block Public Access prevents AMI public sharing but allows cross-account sharing. It also blocks public snapshot sharing except for accounts verified through an external process. This helps prevent accidental public exposure of proprietary AMIs.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative_syntax.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q17

What restriction does the Allowed Images Settings declarative policy enforce?

A. Restricts EC2 instance launches to AMIs from approved AWS accounts or with specific AMI IDs, ensuring only trusted images are used
B. Limits the number of AMIs that can be created per account to prevent storage quota exhaustion
C. Enforces that all AMIs must be encrypted with customer-managed KMS keys before instance launch
D. Requires all AMIs to pass Amazon Inspector vulnerability scans before they can be used

**Answer: A.  Restricts EC2 instance launches to AMIs from approved AWS accounts or with specific AMI IDs, ensuring only trusted images are used**

**Explanation:** Allowed Images Settings restricts which AMIs can be used to launch EC2 instances. You can specify allowed AMI accounts (e.g., only your organization's accounts or AWS marketplace) or specific AMI IDs. This prevents launching instances from untrusted images.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative_syntax.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q18

What does the Instance Metadata Defaults declarative policy configure?

A. Sets default CloudWatch metrics collection interval for all EC2 instances to optimize monitoring costs
B. Enforces IMDSv2 requirements (HttpTokens: required, HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 1) for all new EC2 instances and metadata options modifications
C. Configures default instance tags applied automatically when instances are launched from Account Factory
D. Sets default EBS volume encryption keys used when instances are launched without explicit KMS key specification

**Answer: B.  Enforces IMDSv2 requirements (HttpTokens: required, HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 1) for all new EC2 instances and metadata options modifications**

**Explanation:** Instance Metadata Defaults enforces IMDSv2 (Instance Metadata Service version 2) by setting HttpTokens to 'required' and HttpPutResponseHopLimit to 1. This applies to new instance launches and when metadata options are modified, protecting against SSRF attacks.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative_syntax.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q19

What is the purpose of the Serial Console Access declarative policy?

A. Enables CloudWatch Logs streaming from EC2 serial console output for centralized log management
B. Controls whether account administrators can enable EC2 serial console access for troubleshooting instances without network connectivity
C. Configures automatic serial console session recording for compliance and audit requirements
D. Enforces MFA authentication requirements when accessing instances through the EC2 serial console

**Answer: B.  Controls whether account administrators can enable EC2 serial console access for troubleshooting instances without network connectivity**

**Explanation:** Serial Console Access controls whether account administrators can enable the EC2 serial console feature. Serial console provides troubleshooting access to instances without network connectivity, but can be a security concern. This policy lets you disable it organization-wide.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative_syntax.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q20

What protection does the Snapshot Block Public Access declarative policy provide?

A. Prevents creation of EBS snapshots unless they are encrypted with customer-managed KMS keys
B. Blocks sharing EBS snapshots publicly while allowing private sharing to specific AWS accounts
C. Enforces retention policies on snapshots to prevent premature deletion of backup data
D. Requires Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies to manage all snapshots in the account

**Answer: B.  Blocks sharing EBS snapshots publicly while allowing private sharing to specific AWS accounts**

**Explanation:** Snapshot Block Public Access blocks sharing of EBS snapshots publicly. This prevents accidental public exposure of sensitive data in snapshots. Private sharing to specific AWS accounts is still allowed.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_declarative_syntax.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q21

How do RCPs and SCPs interact to determine effective permissions?

A. SCPs are evaluated first; if allowed, RCPs are then evaluated; both must allow for the action to succeed
B. Effective permissions are the logical intersection of what is allowed by RCPs, SCPs, identity-based policies, and resource-based policies
C. RCPs override SCPs when both are applied; SCPs only take effect when no RCPs are present
D. SCPs apply to member accounts; RCPs apply to the management account; they operate independently

**Answer: B.  Effective permissions are the logical intersection of what is allowed by RCPs, SCPs, identity-based policies, and resource-based policies**

**Explanation:** Effective permissions are the logical intersection (AND operation) of: RCPs, SCPs, identity-based policies, and resource-based policies. All must allow the action for it to succeed. A Deny in any policy type blocks the action.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q22

What should you do before attaching RCPs to the root of your organization?

A. Enable AWS CloudTrail organization trails to monitor all RCP-related API activity
B. Thoroughly test the RCP impact by attaching to individual test accounts first, then OUs, working your way up
C. Create a backup of all IAM policies and resource-based policies in case rollback is needed
D. Submit a service limit increase request to AWS Support for RCP attachment at the root level

**Answer: B.  Thoroughly test the RCP impact by attaching to individual test accounts first, then OUs, working your way up**

**Explanation:** AWS strongly recommends NOT attaching RCPs to the root without thorough testing. Start with individual test accounts, move to OUs lower in the hierarchy, and work your way up. RCPs can break access to resources if not carefully designed.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps.html

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q23

Which statement correctly describes when to use SCPs versus RCPs?

A. Use SCPs when limiting your own principals' permissions; use RCPs when restricting external principals accessing your resources
B. Use SCPs for detective controls; use RCPs for preventive controls in multi-account environments
C. Use SCPs for network-level restrictions; use RCPs for resource-level encryption requirements
D. Use SCPs in development accounts; use RCPs in production accounts for tighter security

**Answer: A.  Use SCPs when limiting your own principals' permissions; use RCPs when restricting external principals accessing your resources**

**Explanation:** Use SCPs to limit what YOUR principals (internal to your organization) can do. Use RCPs to restrict external principals from accessing YOUR resources. Together they create a data perimeter protecting identities and resources.

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q24

What is a key limitation of declarative policies to be aware of?

A. Declarative policies require Enterprise Support plan and incur additional per-account charges
B. Declarative policies currently only support EC2-related services and attributes; other services use SCPs/RCPs
C. Declarative policies cannot be applied to the Security OU containing Log Archive and Audit accounts
D. Declarative policies override IAM policies and can grant permissions even when identity policies deny

**Answer: B.  Declarative policies currently only support EC2-related services and attributes; other services use SCPs/RCPs**

#### Rcp Declarative Policies Q25

What is the maximum size limit for Resource Control Policies (RCPs)?

C. No character limit; RCPs are stored in S3 and referenced by pointer in Organizations

### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q1

What is the primary purpose of AWS IAM Roles Anywhere?

A. To enable on-premises Active Directory integration with AWS services by establishing a domain trust relationship
B. To obtain temporary AWS security credentials for workloads running outside AWS using X.509 certificates and existing IAM roles and policies
C. To provide long-term API keys for external applications that need programmatic access to AWS resources
D. To federate external identity providers like Okta or Azure AD with AWS IAM using SAML 2.0 assertions

**Answer: B.  To obtain temporary AWS security credentials for workloads running outside AWS using X.509 certificates and existing IAM roles and policies**

**Explanation:** IAM Roles Anywhere enables workloads running outside of AWS (servers, containers, applications) to obtain temporary AWS credentials using X.509 certificates. It eliminates the need to manage long-term credentials and uses the same IAM policies and roles as native AWS applications.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/introduction.html

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q2

What is a trust anchor in IAM Roles Anywhere?

A. A reference to a certificate authority (CA) that establishes trust between IAM Roles Anywhere and your PKI infrastructure
B. A designated IAM role in your AWS account that serves as the root for all certificate-based authentication requests
C. A KMS key used to encrypt and decrypt the X.509 certificates presented during authentication to AWS services
D. A VPC endpoint that securely connects your on-premises infrastructure to IAM Roles Anywhere APIs without internet exposure

**Answer: A.  A reference to a certificate authority (CA) that establishes trust between IAM Roles Anywhere and your PKI infrastructure**

**Explanation:** A trust anchor is a reference to either AWS Private CA or an external CA certificate. It establishes trust between IAM Roles Anywhere and your certificate authority. Workloads authenticate using certificates issued by the trusted CA in exchange for temporary AWS credentials.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/introduction.html

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q3

What are the three core components required to use IAM Roles Anywhere?

A. Trust anchor for CA verification, IAM profile defining permissions and session policies, IAM role with trust policy allowing rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com
B. VPC endpoint for private connectivity, KMS key for certificate encryption, IAM user with programmatic access permissions
C. Active Directory domain controller, LDAP connection for authentication, IAM policy granting directory service access to AWS APIs
D. Certificate Signing Request (CSR) generator, AWS Secrets Manager for certificate storage, Lambda function for credential rotation

**Answer: A.  Trust anchor for CA verification, IAM profile defining permissions and session policies, IAM role with trust policy allowing rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com**

**Explanation:** IAM Roles Anywhere requires: (1) Trust anchor referencing your CA, (2) Profile specifying which IAM roles can be assumed and optional session policies, (3) IAM role with a trust policy allowing the rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com service principal and referencing the trust anchor ARN via aws:SourceArn condition.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/introduction.html

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q4

What is the purpose of a profile in IAM Roles Anywhere?

A. A profile stores the X.509 certificates issued to workloads and manages their lifecycle including renewal and revocation
B. A profile specifies which IAM roles can be assumed and defines optional session policies to limit permissions for the session
C. A profile configures the network path for certificate verification including DNS resolvers and proxy servers for CA access
D. A profile defines the CloudWatch log group where all certificate-based authentication attempts are recorded for auditing

**Answer: B.  A profile specifies which IAM roles can be assumed and defines optional session policies to limit permissions for the session**

**Explanation:** A profile in IAM Roles Anywhere specifies which IAM roles workloads can assume and can include session policies (managed or inline) to further limit the permissions granted in the session. A profile can reference multiple IAM roles but only one session policy.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/introduction.html

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q5

How does the IAM Roles Anywhere credential helper tool work?

A. It generates long-term access keys and secret keys from your X.509 certificate and stores them in ~/.aws/credentials file
B. It creates a signature with your certificate, calls IAM Roles Anywhere to obtain temporary session credentials, and returns them in JSON format compatible with credential_process
C. It establishes a persistent VPN tunnel to AWS using your certificate for authentication and proxies all AWS API calls through it
D. It converts your X.509 certificate to a SAML assertion and uses federation to assume roles via AWS STS AssumeRoleWithSAML

**Answer: B.  It creates a signature with your certificate, calls IAM Roles Anywhere to obtain temporary session credentials, and returns them in JSON format compatible with credential_process**

**Explanation:** The credential helper tool creates a signature using your private key and certificate, calls IAM Roles Anywhere to obtain temporary session credentials, and returns them in standard JSON format compatible with the credential_process feature across AWS SDKs. Credentials automatically refresh before expiration.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/credential-helper.html

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q6

What is the trust boundary for IAM Roles Anywhere?

A. Trust is established per VPC - only workloads in trusted VPCs can use certificates to obtain credentials
B. Trust is established at the account level - certificates from any trust anchor in the account can assume any target role in that account unless conditions restrict it
C. Trust is established per region - trust anchors and profiles must be in the same region as the target IAM roles
D. Trust is established at the organization level - certificates are automatically shared across all accounts in the AWS Organization

**Answer: B.  Trust is established at the account level - certificates from any trust anchor in the account can assume any target role in that account unless conditions restrict it**

**Explanation:** For IAM Roles Anywhere, the trust boundary is at the account level. Certificates issued by any trust anchor in the account can be used to assume any target role in that same account, unless you specify conditions in the role's trust policy to restrict access further.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/introduction.html

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q7

Which advanced key storage mechanisms does the IAM Roles Anywhere credential helper support?

A. Only file-based private keys stored as PEM files in the local filesystem with optional passphrase protection
B. OS certificate stores (Windows CNG/Cryptography API, macOS Keychain), PKCS#11 hardware tokens/HSMs, and TPM-based keys
C. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store for encrypted storage and AWS Secrets Manager for automatic rotation of private keys
D. HashiCorp Vault integration for dynamic secret generation and Kubernetes secret volumes for container-based workloads

**Answer: B.  OS certificate stores (Windows CNG/Cryptography API, macOS Keychain), PKCS#11 hardware tokens/HSMs, and TPM-based keys**

**Explanation:** The credential helper supports advanced key storage: (1) OS certificate stores on Windows and macOS, (2) PKCS#11 tokens and HSMs using PKCS#11 URIs, (3) TPM (Trusted Platform Module) keys for hardware-backed security. This enables secure key management beyond simple file storage.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/credential-helper.html

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q8

How can you restrict which certificates can assume a specific IAM role using IAM Roles Anywhere?

A. Configure the trust anchor to only accept certificates with specific organizational units in the subject distinguished name
B. Add conditions to the role's trust policy based on certificate attributes mapped to principal tags (e.g., x509Issuer/CN, x509Subject/O)
C. Implement a Lambda authorizer that validates certificate serial numbers against a DynamoDB whitelist before allowing role assumption
D. Use AWS Certificate Manager to create a certificate revocation list and configure IAM to check it during authentication

**Answer: B.  Add conditions to the role's trust policy based on certificate attributes mapped to principal tags (e.g., x509Issuer/CN, x509Subject/O)**

**Explanation:** You can add conditions to the role's trust policy that check certificate attributes. The profile's attribute mapping controls which X.509 certificate fields (issuer, subject, SAN) are mapped to principal tags. The trust policy can then use conditions like aws:PrincipalTag/x509Issuer/CN to restrict access based on certificate attributes.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/attribute-mapping-and-trust-policy.html

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q9

What happens if your profile's attribute mapping doesn't map a certificate field that your role's trust policy condition checks?

A. IAM Roles Anywhere will automatically map all certificate fields to principal tags regardless of the attribute mapping configuration
B. The condition will evaluate to false (for StringEquals) or true (for StringNotEquals) because the principal tag doesn't exist
C. An explicit error will be returned stating that the certificate is missing required attributes for the role
D. The certificate validation will fail and the trust anchor will be automatically disabled to prevent security issues

**Answer: B.  The condition will evaluate to false (for StringEquals) or true (for StringNotEquals) because the principal tag doesn't exist**

**Explanation:** If a profile's attribute mapping doesn't include a specifier for a field (e.g., CN), that field won't be mapped to principal tags. A StringEquals condition checking that tag evaluates to false (denying access), while StringNotEquals evaluates to true (granting access) - be careful with negated conditions!

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/attribute-mapping-and-trust-policy.html

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q10

How does IAM Roles Anywhere integrate with AWS PrivateLink?

A. IAM Roles Anywhere automatically creates VPC endpoints in all VPCs where workloads need certificate-based authentication
B. You can create interface VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) to establish private connections to IAM Roles Anywhere APIs without internet access
C. PrivateLink is mandatory for IAM Roles Anywhere - all certificate verification must occur over private VPC connections
D. IAM Roles Anywhere uses PrivateLink internally to communicate with AWS Private CA for certificate validation

**Answer: B.  You can create interface VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) to establish private connections to IAM Roles Anywhere APIs without internet access**

**Explanation:** IAM Roles Anywhere supports interface VPC endpoints via AWS PrivateLink, allowing you to establish private connections between your VPCs and IAM Roles Anywhere APIs. This enables workloads to obtain credentials without traversing the internet.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/rolesanywhere/latest/userguide/vpc-interface-endpoints.html

#### Rolesanywhere Directoryservice Q11

What notification capabilities does IAM Roles Anywhere provide for certificate lifecycle management?

A. Email notifications sent directly from IAM Roles Anywhere to administrators when certificates are within 30 days of expiration
B. Notifications sent to AWS Health, CloudWatch Events, and EventBridge for trust anchor and end-entity certificate expiry events
C. SMS alerts via SNS when certificates expire, including automatic escalation to on-call engineers if not renewed within 48 hours
D. Integration with AWS Certificate Manager for automatic certificate renewal and deployment to IAM Roles Anywhere trust anchors

**Answer: B.  Notifications sent to AWS Health, CloudWatch Events, and EventBridge for trust anchor and end-entity certificate expiry events**

**Explanation:** IAM Roles Anywhere sends notifications through AWS Health, CloudWatch Events, and EventBridge for certificate expiry events (both trust anchor CA certificates and end-entity workload certificates). You can customize notification thresholds and create automated remediation workflows.

Which Directory Service option is a standalone managed directory powered by Samba 4 Active Directory Compatible Server?

B. Simple AD is a Samba 4-based standalone directory with a subset of AD features, supporting up to 5,000 users in the large edition

What is the primary difference between AD Connector and AWS Managed Microsoft AD?

A. AD Connector redirects authentication requests to on-premises AD without caching data; AWS Managed Microsoft AD is an actual Microsoft AD domain controller managed by AWS
B. AD Connector provides read-only access to on-premises AD; AWS Managed Microsoft AD provides full read-write access with synchronization
C. AD Connector requires VPN connectivity to on-premises infrastructure; AWS Managed Microsoft AD works entirely within AWS without external dependencies
D. AD Connector supports up to 500,000 users; AWS Managed Microsoft AD (Enterprise Edition) is limited to 30,000 directory objects

**Answer: A.  AD Connector redirects authentication requests to on-premises AD without caching data; AWS Managed Microsoft AD is an actual Microsoft AD domain controller managed by AWS**

**Explanation:** AD Connector is a directory gateway that redirects requests to your on-premises Microsoft Active Directory without caching information. AWS Managed Microsoft AD is an actual Microsoft AD domain controller running in AWS Cloud, managed by AWS as a service.

What type of trust relationships can AWS Managed Microsoft AD establish?

B. Resource forest trusts with your existing AD domains on-premises, in AWS, or in multi-cloud environments for seamless user access

### Route53 Resolver Logs

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q1

What does Route 53 VPC Resolver query logging capture?

A. Only DNS queries to malicious domains
B. DNS queries that originate in your VPCs
C. Only queries to public hosted zones
D. API calls to the Route 53 Resolver service

**Answer: B.  DNS queries that originate in your VPCs**

**Explanation:** VPC Resolver query logging captures DNS queries that originate in your VPCs. To start logging, you create a query logging configuration and associate it with VPCs or a Route 53 Profile. Logs appear within a few minutes.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-query-logging-configurations-managing.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q2

To which AWS resources can you send VPC Resolver query logs?

A. Only Amazon CloudWatch Logs
B. Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group, Amazon S3 bucket, or Firehose delivery stream
C. Only Amazon S3 for long-term retention
D. Only Amazon Security Lake

**Answer: B.  Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group, Amazon S3 bucket, or Firehose delivery stream**

**Explanation:** You can send VPC Resolver query logs to: CloudWatch Logs (Logs Insights, metrics, alarms), S3 (economical for long-term archiving), or Firehose (real-time streaming to OpenSearch, Redshift, or other applications).

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-query-logs-choosing-target-resource.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q3

How can you associate VPC Resolver query logging with VPCs?

A. Only by selecting individual VPCs in the console
B. Direct VPC association or by associating the configuration to a Route 53 Profile (which applies to all VPCs associated with that Profile)
C. Only through CloudFormation; no console option
D. By enabling DNS logging on each subnet separately

**Answer: B.  Direct VPC association or by associating the configuration to a Route 53 Profile (which applies to all VPCs associated with that Profile)**

**Explanation:** You can configure query logging in two ways: (1) Direct VPC association—associate VPCs directly to the query logging configuration, or (2) Profile association—associate the configuration to a Route 53 Profile, which applies logging to all VPCs associated with that Profile.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-query-logging-configurations-managing.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q4

What region requirement exists when creating a Resolver query logging configuration?

A. The configuration can be in any region; logs flow globally
B. The configuration must be in the same Region as the VPCs you want to log queries for; create at least one config per Region for multi-region VPCs
C. The configuration must be in us-east-1 only
D. The S3 or CloudWatch destination determines the region; VPC region does not matter

**Answer: B.  The configuration must be in the same Region as the VPCs you want to log queries for; create at least one config per Region for multi-region VPCs**

**Explanation:** The query logging configuration must be in the same Region where you created the VPCs you want to log. If you have VPCs in multiple Regions, you must create at least one query logging configuration for each Region.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-query-logging-configurations-managing.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q5

What limitation applies to VPC log delivery destinations?

A. You can deliver to unlimited destinations of each type
B. VPC log delivery can be enabled only once for a specific destination type; you cannot deliver to multiple destinations of the same type (e.g., two S3 buckets)
C. You must use both CloudWatch and S3 together
D. Firehose is required for all configurations

**Answer: B.  VPC log delivery can be enabled only once for a specific destination type; you cannot deliver to multiple destinations of the same type (e.g., two S3 buckets)**

**Explanation:** VPC log delivery can be enabled only once for a specific destination type. The logs cannot be delivered to multiple destinations of the same type—for example, VPC logs cannot be delivered to two Amazon S3 buckets.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-query-logging-configurations-managing.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q6

For workloads with high queries per second (QPS), which destination is recommended to avoid throttling?

A. CloudWatch Logs only; it has the highest throughput
B. Amazon S3 to ensure query logs are not throttled when written; CloudWatch PutLogEvents can be increased but S3 is preferred for high QPS
C. Firehose only
D. Split logs across multiple CloudWatch log groups

**Answer: B.  Amazon S3 to ensure query logs are not throttled when written; CloudWatch PutLogEvents can be increased but S3 is preferred for high QPS**

**Explanation:** If you expect high QPS, use Amazon S3 to ensure your query logs are not throttled. With CloudWatch, you can request an increase to the PutLogEvents limit, but S3 is the recommended choice for high-volume workloads.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-query-logs-choosing-target-resource.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q7

When sending query logs to an S3 bucket with SSE-KMS encryption, what is required?

B. Update the KMS key policy so the log delivery account can write to your S3 bucket
C. Use only S3-managed keys (SSE-S3); SSE-KMS is not supported
D. Create a separate KMS key in each account that sends logs

**Answer: B.  Update the KMS key policy so the log delivery account can write to your S3 bucket**

**Explanation:** If you choose Server-Side Encryption with AWS KMS Keys (SSE-KMS), you must update the key policy for your customer managed key so that the log delivery account can write to your Amazon S3 bucket.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-query-logs-choosing-target-resource.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q8

For a central S3 bucket storing query logs across the organization, what approach does AWS recommend?

A. Each account sends logs directly to the central bucket with cross-account permissions
B. Set up the query logging configuration from a centralized account (with permissions to write to the central bucket) and use RAM to share the configuration across accounts
C. Use a single account and peer all VPCs into it
D. Use Firehose to aggregate logs before S3 delivery

**Answer: B.  Set up the query logging configuration from a centralized account (with permissions to write to the central bucket) and use RAM to share the configuration across accounts**

**Explanation:** To store logs in a central S3 bucket for your organization, AWS recommends setting up the query logging configuration from a centralized account (with permissions to write to the central bucket) and using AWS RAM to share the configuration across accounts.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-query-logs-choosing-target-resource.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q9

How do you share a Resolver query logging configuration with other AWS accounts?

A. Using IAM cross-account roles only
B. Using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM); the Route 53 console integrates with RAM for sharing
C. Sharing is not supported; each account must create its own configuration
D. Using AWS Organizations SCPs to propagate the configuration

**Answer: B.  Using AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM); the Route 53 console integrates with RAM for sharing**

**Explanation:** You can share query logging configurations using AWS Resource Access Manager. The Route 53 VPC Resolver console integrates with RAM. Accounts that receive a shared configuration can associate their VPCs with it.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/query-logging-configurations-managing-sharing.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q10

What permission is required to share a Resolver query logging configuration with another account?

A. route53:ShareConfiguration
B. route53resolver:PutResolverQueryLogConfigPolicy
C. iam:CreateRole
D. ram:CreateResourceShare only

**Answer: B.  route53resolver:PutResolverQueryLogConfigPolicy**

**Explanation:** To share a query logging configuration with another AWS account, you must have permission to use the PutResolverQueryLogConfigPolicy action.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/query-logging-configurations-managing-sharing.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q11

What can an account that receives a shared query logging configuration do?

A. Change or delete the configuration
B. Associate VPCs with the configuration; it cannot change or delete the rule
C. Add or remove tags on the configuration
D. Modify the destination (CloudWatch, S3, or Firehose) of the shared configuration

**Answer: B.  Associate VPCs with the configuration; it cannot change or delete the rule**

**Explanation:** The account that receives a shared configuration can associate its VPCs with the configuration. However, the account cannot change or delete the configuration. Only the creator can add, delete, or see tags.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/query-logging-configurations-managing-sharing.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q12

What is Route 53 VPC Resolver and where does it operate?

A. A global DNS service for public hosted zones only
B. A recursive DNS resolver available by default in all VPCs; it answers queries for public records, VPC-specific names, and private hosted zones
C. A VPN-based DNS proxy for on-premises networks
D. A DNS firewall that blocks malicious domains

**Answer: B.  A recursive DNS resolver available by default in all VPCs; it answers queries for public records, VPC-specific names, and private hosted zones**

**Explanation:** Route 53 VPC Resolver responds recursively to DNS queries for public records, VPC-specific DNS names, and private hosted zones. It is available by default in all VPCs. A VPC connects to it at the VPC+2 IP address.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q13

What is a primary security use case for Route 53 DNS Firewall (which works with Resolver)?

A. Blocking inbound DDoS attacks on DNS
B. Helping prevent DNS exfiltration by filtering and regulating outbound DNS traffic from your VPCs
C. Encrypting DNS queries with TLS
D. Replacing VPC Flow Logs for network visibility

**Answer: B.  Helping prevent DNS exfiltration by filtering and regulating outbound DNS traffic from your VPCs**

**Explanation:** DNS Firewall helps prevent DNS exfiltration—when a compromised instance uses DNS lookups to send data to a domain the attacker controls. You can monitor and control which domains applications can query, deny known-bad domains, or allow only trusted domains.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-dns-firewall.html

#### Route53 Resolver Logs Q14

How does DNS Firewall differ from AWS Network Firewall regarding DNS traffic?

A. They are identical; both filter DNS the same way
B. DNS Firewall filters outbound DNS queries through VPC Resolver; Network Firewall does not have visibility into queries made by VPC Resolver
C. Network Firewall replaces DNS Firewall for all DNS filtering
D. DNS Firewall only works with public hosted zones

**Answer: B.  DNS Firewall filters outbound DNS queries through VPC Resolver; Network Firewall does not have visibility into queries made by VPC Resolver**

**Explanation:** DNS Firewall filters outbound DNS queries that pass through Route 53 VPC Resolver. Network Firewall filters network and application layer traffic but does not have visibility into queries made by VPC Resolver. They address different paths.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-dns-firewall.html

What pricing applies to VPC Resolver query logging?

A. Resolver query logging is free
B. CloudWatch Vended Logs charges apply when using VPC Resolver logs, even when logs are published directly to S3
C. Only S3 storage charges apply; no CloudWatch charges
D. Charges apply only when using Firehose

**Answer: B.  CloudWatch Vended Logs charges apply when using VPC Resolver logs, even when logs are published directly to S3**

**Explanation:** CloudWatch Vended Logs charges apply when using VPC Resolver logs, even when logs are published directly to Amazon S3. See CloudWatch pricing and Logs/Vended Logs for details.

Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resolver-query-logs-choosing-target-resource.html

When sending logs to an S3 bucket in an account you do not own, what must the bucket owner add to their bucket policy?
